Tech Report: Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain

📅 26 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (817 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a new generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity.
  • A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides new insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them.
  • Most of the research was conducted at the Institute of Physics at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, with contributions from a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a new generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity. Although most people have never heard of skyrmions, these microscopic magnetic vortices may eventually play an key role in how computers store and process data.

A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides new insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them. The findings could help researchers develop smaller, more efficient computing systems and advance emerging quantum technologies.

Most of the research was conducted at the Institute of Physics at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, with contributions from a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).

"Skyrmions are small, magnetic vortices that can store information in a completely new way," explained Asle Sudbø, who leads NTNU's Centre for Quantum Spintronics (QuSpin).

Unlike conventional technologies, which require increasing amounts of space and energy to handle growing quantities of data, skyrmions could offer a much more efficient alternative.

"Instead of the current technology, where we constantly need more space and energy to process data, skyrmions could make it possible to build much smaller and more energy-efficient data storage systems," explained Sudbø.

Tiny Magnetic Vortices Could Enable Brain-Like Computers.

In a recent development, the potential applications of skyrmions extend well beyond conventional data storage. They are also important to spintronics, which explores ways to use the magnetic properties of electrons in electronic devices, and to research involving topological quantum effects.

One particularly promising possibility is the development of computers that operate in ways similar to biological brains.

"These nanoscale vortices could help develop computers that resemble biological brains," stated Sudbø.

It has been revealed that rather than relying on conventional transistor-based computing, such systems could use magnetism to process information. In principle, this approach could dramatically reduce electricity consumption, potentially allowing future computers to perform complex tasks with very little energy.

Turning that possibility into practical technology, however, requires scientists to understand exactly how skyrmions behave and how to manipulate them reliably.

The latest research represents an notable advance toward that goal.

Scientists Film Magnetic Skyrmion Lattices Melting for the First Time.

Sources indicate that skyrmions do not always exist as isolated magnetic structures. Under certain conditions, they organize themselves into repeating patterns known as lattices, resembling the orderly arrangement of atoms in a crystal, but on a much smaller scale.

Scientists can manipulate these arrangements, a capability that could be essential for using skyrmions in future computing devices.

In the latest study, researchers achieved something that had not been demonstrated before. They recorded the melting of a magnetic skyrmion lattice as it happened while simultaneously controlling individual skyrmions.

"For the first time, researchers have managed to film how a magnetic skyrmion lattice melts in real time, while simultaneously being able to manipulate each individual skyrmion directly as they film it. For example, both their shape and size can be changed 'on the fly'," remarked Sudbø.

Recent findings suggest that the ability to observe this process directly provides a clearer picture of how skyrmions respond when their organized structures break apart. It also allows researchers to study how changing the size and shape of individual magnetic vortices affects their behavior.

A New Step Toward Energy-Efficient Computing.

Recent findings suggest that understanding how skyrmions behave during the breakdown of their lattices could help scientists develop more precise ways to control them. That control is particularly vital if these magnetic structures are to become useful components in future computer systems.

The findings therefore offer more than a newly introduced way to observe an unusual magnetic phenomenon. They provide information that could help researchers overcome challenges involved in developing practical skyrmion-based technologies.

Recent findings suggest that "The findings give us new insight into how these types of particles behave. This could therefore become important for the development of more energy-efficient computer technology in the future," said Sudbø.

Although substantial development is still needed before skyrmions can be used in everyday computing devices, the research highlights their potential for improving data storage, enabling new computing architectures, and supporting advances in quantum technology.

By learning to observe and manipulate these tiny magnetic vortices in real time, scientists are gaining capabilities that could eventually help reshape the design of computers.

"This could revolutionize the way we think about computers," concluded Sudbø.

#115761. Latest Update: A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2337 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2337 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it?
  • Industry observers note that researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself.
  • It has been revealed that the research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it? Unlike the bits used in ordinary computers, quantum bits, or qubits, are extraordinarily sensitive to measurement. Trying to determine their state can cause that state to collapse, potentially erasing the very information scientists want to retrieve.

Industry observers note that researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself. Their approach focuses on a special type known as an "Andreev qubit," which can generate an oscillating electric supercurrent through its own quantum behavior. By monitoring this current, scientists may be able to determine the qubit's state without directly measuring it or significantly disturbing the information it contains.

It has been revealed that the research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters. It was led by José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil, and Yugui Yao of the School of Physics at the Beijing Institute of Technology in China. If experimentally confirmed, their method could simplify quantum computing by removing the need for extra qubits used in certain measurement techniques.

Why Measuring Quantum Information Is So Difficult.

According to recent reports, conventional computers store information in bits that have one of two values, 0 or 1. These values can be checked repeatedly without changing the information. Quantum computers work differently because their qubits can exist in superpositions, meaning they can combine the states 0 and 1 in ways that are not possible with conventional bits.

This unusual ability is central to the potential power of quantum computing. However, it also creates a major vulnerability. Quantum states can be disrupted by interactions with their surroundings, including the instruments scientists use to examine them.

"In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained," indicates Egues.

Sources indicate that to minimize this problem, physicists developed techniques known as "quantum nondemolition measurements," or QND. Many of these approaches use an additional quantum system called an ancilla. Rather than measuring the original qubit directly, researchers transfer information to the ancilla and measure that auxiliary system instead.

According to recent reports, the term "ancilla" comes from a Latin word meaning "slave" or "servant." In modern scientific usage, it describes something that performs a supporting function. Here, the ancilla acts as an intermediary, allowing researchers to obtain information while preserving the original qubit as much as possible.

According to recent reports, although effective, these procedures come with practical disadvantages. Scientists must prepare the auxiliary qubits, connect them to the qubits being studied, transfer information between them, and perform repeated measurements. These additional steps require time and equipment, and the complexity becomes increasingly significant as the number of qubits grows.

Recent findings suggest that "Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself," claims the researcher.

A Special Quantum Bit That Produces Its Own Signal.

In a recent development, the proposed technique relies on the unusual properties of an Andreev qubit. Its name honors Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939-2023), who identified a distinctive quantum process in 1964 that occurs where normal materials meet superconductors.

Sources indicate that superconductors are materials that can conduct electricity without electrical resistance under appropriate conditions. At the boundaries involving these materials, special quantum states known as "Andreev states" can form. In the system studied by the researchers, these states are confined to an extremely small region between two superconducting materials.

These quantum states can represent the basic values 0 and 1, along with superpositions of those values, making them suitable for storing quantum information.

"In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot - that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined - formed in an indium arsenide [InAs] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It's in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed," Egues explains.

The key to the new approach is an electrical phenomenon called a "supercurrent." Unlike the current flowing through ordinary electrical conductors, a supercurrent moves without resistance.

The researchers found that when the Andreev qubit exists in a superposition, the supercurrent develops a component that oscillates over time. These fluctuations arise from quantum interference between the different states making up the superposition.

Sources indicate that crucially, the oscillations are not random. Their behavior contains information about the qubit's underlying quantum state, potentially allowing scientists to determine what that state is without directly measuring the qubit.

Recent findings suggest that "It's precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It's that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal," the researcher points out.

How a Tiny Electrical Current Reveals Quantum Information.

To understand how the technique works, it helps to consider how physicists describe a qubit's state mathematically.

Sources indicate that one common representation is the "Bloch sphere," a geometric model in which every possible pure state of a single qubit corresponds to a point on the surface of a sphere. Two angles determine the location of that point.

It has been revealed that the first angle describes how much each of the two basic states contributes to the superposition. The second describes their relative phase, which specifies how the quantum components are aligned with one another. Together, these two measurements provide the information needed to identify the qubit's state.

According to the upcoming research, both pieces of information can be extracted from the supercurrent. Its steady component and the size of its oscillations reveal the relative contributions of the two basic states. Meanwhile, the timing of the oscillations provides information about their phase relationship.

It has been revealed that "Our study showed that this information is encoded in the supercurrent itself. The supercurrent has a constant component and a fluctuating component. The value of the constant component and the amplitude of the oscillation reveal the proportion of each state (0 and 1) in the superposition, and the moment when that oscillation begins reveals the phase relationship between them. Thus, by measuring how the current varies over time, it's possible to reconstruct the initial state of the qubit," Egues explains.

Sources indicate that this means the electrical current effectively carries a signature of the quantum information stored in the system. By observing how that signature changes over time, researchers could reconstruct the qubit's original state.

A Supercurrent That Oscillates Without Voltage.

Another surprising feature of the proposed system is that the electrical current can oscillate without an externally applied voltage.

Ordinarily, producing an oscillating supercurrent in this type of superconducting system requires a voltage. This familiar phenomenon is called the "AC Josephson effect.".

In a recent development, the researchers predict something different in their Andreev qubit. Here, the current's oscillations arise naturally from the qubit's own quantum evolution. No outside voltage is required to generate them.

"Our system generates a supercurrent that varies over time like an alternating current but without voltage. It's the very evolution of the qubit's state that produces that oscillation," states Egues.

This behavior is key because it transforms quantum activity occurring on an extraordinarily small scale into a detectable electrical signal. The current provides a connection between the microscopic world of quantum states and the larger physical systems scientists can measure.

That connection is what makes the proposed reading technique possible.

Detecting Quantum States With an Extremely Sensitive Sensor.

The researchers envision placing the Andreev qubit inside a closed superconducting circuit, allowing its supercurrent to circulate continuously.

Next to the circuit would sit a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device), a highly sensitive instrument capable of detecting extremely weak magnetic fields.

Whenever an electric current flows, it produces a magnetic field. Because the supercurrent in this system oscillates, the magnetic field it generates also changes over time.

Recent findings suggest that the nearby SQUID could detect these tiny magnetic variations and use them to determine the behavior of the circulating current. Since the current contains information about the qubit's quantum state, the researchers could then reconstruct that state without measuring the qubit directly.

Egues compares the arrangement to two compasses that interact through a magnetic field.

It has been revealed that "We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID 'senses' that field. Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small.".

The weak interaction between the sensor and the qubit is especially key. It offers a way to gather information while minimizing the disturbance that normally accompanies quantum measurements.

Reading Quantum Information With Almost No Disturbance.

According to recent reports, in quantum physics, observing a system is not necessarily a harmless process. A measuring instrument interacts with whatever it is attempting to measure, and that interaction can change the system's behavior.

Sources indicate that this fundamental difficulty puzzled the earliest researchers studying quantum mechanics. It remains an unavoidable feature of quantum measurements today.

In a recent development, the proposed technique does not eliminate this effect entirely. The SQUID still interacts with the circuit, creating a small amount of feedback that can influence the qubit. However, the team's simulations suggest that this disturbance can be reduced to a level so small that it becomes effectively negligible.

"Our method doesn't eliminate the fundamental problem of quantum measurement. But it can approach the limit of a non-destructive readout and, at the same time, avoid the use of auxiliary qubits - the ancillas - employed in other non-destructive quantum measurement protocols," Egues notes.

It has been revealed that the approach could also remove another complication found in some existing techniques. Because researchers would not need to restore the qubit to its original state after every measurement, they could make repeated observations as the state changes.

This would allow scientists to follow the qubit's quantum evolution over time, rather than obtaining information only through separate measurement and reset cycles.

Simulations Achieve Up to 99.85% Accuracy.

To investigate whether the method could work outside ideal theoretical conditions, the researchers performed computer simulations designed to account for imperfections that would arise in real experiments.

These calculations included measurement noise, as well as the small amount of feedback introduced by the detection coil. The goal was to determine whether the qubit's state could still be reconstructed accurately despite these disturbances.

It has been revealed that the results were encouraging. Depending on the number of measurements used, the simulations produced accuracies of 99.52%, 99.81%, and 99.85%.

According to the researchers, these values fall within the standard thresholds used in quantum error correction schemes, which are designed to manage errors in quantum information processing.

The findings suggest that the method could provide highly accurate quantum state reconstruction without the additional complexity of auxiliary qubits.

Industry observers note that however, the technique has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. The results come entirely from theoretical analysis and computer simulations, so researchers still need to establish whether a physical device can achieve comparable performance.

Could This Make Quantum Computers Simpler?

Despite the lack of experimental confirmation, the researchers emphasize that their proposal does not depend on technologies that have yet to be invented.

The calculations use realistic properties drawn from existing quantum systems, and SQUID sensors are already established tools for detecting exceptionally weak magnetic fields and electric currents.

What remains to be built is the specific arrangement of components required to implement the proposed measurement technique.

"All the numbers we used are realistic. In principle, this can be achieved. In fact, we used parameters from existing systems in our calculations. What doesn't yet exist is that geometry, that setup that we proposed," he argues.

According to recent reports, this makes the approach different from theoretical concepts that cannot be realized until scientists develop entirely newly introduced materials or manufacturing techniques. In principle, the necessary components already exist, although assembling them into the proposed configuration and demonstrating the predicted behavior remain key challenges.

The research offers two potentially significant advances.

According to recent reports, from the standpoint of fundamental physics, it predicts that a qubit can produce an oscillating supercurrent resembling the AC Josephson effect, but without requiring an external voltage. Instead, the oscillations emerge from the qubit's own coherent quantum evolution.

Sources indicate that from a technological perspective, the study reveals how those oscillations could serve as a measurable signature of the qubit's internal state. By analyzing the electrical current, researchers could recover quantum information while causing very little disturbance to the system.

Recent findings suggest that if future experiments confirm these predictions, the method could make reading Andreev qubits substantially simpler. Eliminating auxiliary qubits and repeated resets could reduce the equipment and procedures needed to retrieve quantum information.

More fundamentally, the work points toward an intriguing possibility: information hidden in the microscopic quantum world may be accessible through an electrical current produced by the quantum system itself, offering a promising upcoming way to observe delicate quantum states without destroying them.

Huawei convicted of money laundering, conspiracy to steal trade secrets, and fraud by US jury

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (630 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A jury has found Huawei guilty of bank fraud, wire fraud, money laundering conspiracy, conspiracy to steal trade secrets, and violations of the U.S.
  • “Today’s verdict makes clear that fraud, sanctions evasion, and the theft of intellectual property are not business strategies, they are serious crimes,” James Barnacle, the Assistant Director in Charge of the FBI New York Field Office, which conducted the investigation on the tech firm, told the publication.
  • Huawei has long been in the crosshairs of the U.S., with the manufacturer getting banned from the country in 2018 alongside other Chinese telecommunications hardware manufacturers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A jury has found Huawei guilty of bank fraud, wire fraud, money laundering conspiracy, conspiracy to steal trade secrets, and violations of the U.S. sanctions against Iran, among others. According to Bloomberg, the verdict was the result of a nearly three-month trial in which a foreign company has been prosecuted by the U.S. Department of Justice. This is a rare occurrence, resulting in a conviction of 10 out of 12 counts, with the Chinese company getting cleared of conspiracy to obstruct justice and racketeering conspiracy.

“Today’s verdict makes clear that fraud, sanctions evasion, and the theft of intellectual property are not business strategies, they are serious crimes,” James Barnacle, the Assistant Director in Charge of the FBI New York Field Office, which conducted the investigation on the tech firm, told the publication. “Huawei’s success was built on deception and theft, and the FBI will never hesitate to pursue those who profit by breaking the law.”.

Huawei has long been in the crosshairs of the U.S., with the manufacturer getting banned from the country in 2018 alongside other Chinese telecommunications hardware manufacturers. It has even sued the U.S. government, claiming that the equipment ban against the company is unconstitutional. Nevertheless, Washington proceeded with the move and built a case against the company as early as 2019. This has been hit by multiple delays, though, owing to the COVID-19 Pandemic, as well as Huawei’s multiple attempts to halt the investigation even before the case went to trial. There was even an allegation that two Chinese intelligence officers offered $61,000 in Bitcoin to a U.S. law enforcement official to get insider information about the case.

According to recent reports, it was also in 2018 that the daughter of Huawei founder and manufacturer CFO Meng Wanzhou was arrested in Canada on suspicion of the firm’s attempt to circumvent U.S. sanctions on Iran. Washington even attempted to have her extradited to the U.S., but she was able to return to China in 2019 after admitting to the company’s illegal business in Iran. Aside from that, the U.S. Department of Justice provided other examples of Huawei’s violations, including the theft of T-Mobile’s robotic touch screen testing robot, with a Huawei employee stealing a part of the device from T-Mobile’s controlled lab, the copying of Cisco router source code, another Huawei employee photographing proprietary Fujitsu equipment, and using confidential information gathered through an NDA from Quintel, a U.S. antenna manufacturer, which was subsequently included in Huawei’s patent application.

On the other hand, the company’s lead defense attorney, Brian Heberlig, focused on its acquittal on two of the charges. “It’s hard not to have profoundly mixed emotions from the verdict we just heard,” Heberlig told Bloomberg. The racketeering conspiracy “alleged that the company was corrupt from top to bottom, that it had a corporate culture and policy of cheating, stealing, and lying, and the jury found the company not guilty on that charge.”.

According to recent reports, sentencing hearing for the company is set for September 2027, although it’s still unclear what penalties the U.S. government is seeking. The Chinese Foreign Ministry, on the other hand, mentioned, “The Chinese government firmly opposes the U.S. suppression and containment of Chinese companies and firmly supports Chinese companies in safeguarding their legitimate rights and interests.”.

Coca-Cola ditched AI for its fresh holiday ad

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (937 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After two years of AI-generated holiday ads that spawned plenty of real-world backlash, Coca-Cola went live-action for its latest holiday campaign.
  • After two years of AI-generated holiday ads that spawned plenty of real-world backlash, Coca-Cola went live-action for its latest holiday campaign.
  • Recent findings suggest that coca-Cola’s latest spot “Enjoy Joy” indicates real human actors as friends and family engaged in fall and winter activities, like playing football and having a turkey dinner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After two years of AI-generated holiday ads that spawned plenty of real-world backlash, Coca-Cola went live-action for its latest holiday campaign. Coca-Cola’s fresh spot “Enjoy Joy” indicates real human actors as friends and family engaged in fall and winter activities, like playing football and having a turkey dinner. It ends with the word Enjoy written in its new tall, serifed typeface. Directed by Paul Dektor and produced by Mayan Productions, the commercial builds on last year’s “Refresh Your Holidays” campaign meant to position the soft drink brand as a point of connection between people during the holiday season. Unlike last year’s advertising, however, it’s human-made. A spokesperson for Coca-Cola tells Fast Tech giant the spot was created without the use of generative AI. This year, brands have gone to great lengths to prove their ads aren’t AI as public opinion turns against the technology. Apple, Levi’s, Prada, and others took an analog, handcrafted approach to their recent advertising, and Coca-Cola is another data point in a trend. Still, the company says viewers shouldn’t read into the choice too much. “This does not signal a broader shift, as Coca-Cola continues to explore different creative approaches and emerging technologies to bring its storytelling to life,” says Madison Chandler, a spokesperson for the company. “Human storytellers remain at the center of the creative process, with AI serving as a tool to support and enhance creative expression where appropriate.” Coca-Cola was an early adopter to AI marketing, offering an online, AI-generated holiday card maker in 2023. It followed that up with its AI-generated remakes of “Holidays Are Coming” in 2024. Despite online criticism, it released yet another AI-generated ad last year that showed AI-generated snowscapes, winter creatures, and localized elements for geo-specific media buys, like a “Welcome to Boston” billboard in Boston. While Coca-Cola’s AI-generated ads were picked apart on social media, the company remarked those spots actually passed its own Christmas ad benchmarks. Pratik Thakar, Coca‑Cola’s global head of generative AI, has said the ads were a proof point for the possibilities of creating personalized, programmatic content at scale. Good numbers or not, it’s hard to deny that there’s been a vibe shift in the perception of AI advertising. An August Gallup poll found 62% of U.S. adults believe it’s “very” or “somewhat unacceptable” for businesses to use AI to create people or voices in ads, and 46% said the same thing about using AI to create the final text, image, or video. In 2024, market research firm NielsenIQ found that AI-generated advertising may have a negative brand halo, and that it elicits weaker memory activation. This year, Coca-Cola decided to embrace the trend and go human-made. But 2027? It’s a whole new year, and a whole new ad landscape.

I really prefer the dongle style streamer that hides behind the TV vs a bulky box like the current one.

I'm guessing the next one will also be bulky.

According to recent reports, on October 29, the Google Home release notes had a Device Firmware section that mentioned the enhancement for both the 4K and HD models. Compared to the original changelog, Google added “Connectivity, media streaming, and display performance improvements.”.

Original 10/12: According to Google’s release notes, UTTA.260813.002 is rolling out just for the 4K model. There is no latest release for the HD variant today. Both streaming devices are usually updated at the same time.

Industry observers note that this update bumps the Android Security Patch Level to August 2026 (from October 2025). Google also notes the presence of “Other bug fixes and performance improvements.”.

On your Chromecast with Google TV, go to Settings > System > About > System update to download and install.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that somewhere inside a hollowed-out volcano, a bald man stroking a white cat is playing a Barry White LP and dimming down his lair’s halogens with the F4 lighting console. Or perhaps operating an orbital weapon. I want one. The control panel. The orbital weapon, too. Maybe a synthetic polar bear rug while we’re at it. Designed and made by Sacrebleu, a one-person workshop in Washington state run by Alex Dufetel, the F4 is a home automation console that resembles a tiny audio mixing board. The 13 x 7.5 x 3.5-inch device has four motorized faders, a fat aluminum knob, four metal keys, and a small screen, all wrapped in walnut. [Photo: Sacrebleu] It costs $1,700. It does absolutely nothing my phone can’t already do, but who cares. I just can’t resist the ’70s vibes. And physical controls are just better. While manufacturers avoid them to save on costs, many people want them back. As Dufetel tells me, “Our hands want physical feedback: something to push against, and a response they can feel.” Dufetel used to run a Meta team working on how people interact with virtual and augmented reality (remember Zuck’s metaverse?). The F4 is 2,000% a much better use of his talent and time. Just look at the faders. They work like the motorized sliders on a big recording studio desk. They move by themselves. If you dim your original 1962 Flos Arco lamp—because, if you have $1,700 to sink into a lighting console, you have an original Arco lamp—in your living room using your phone’s home automation app, the matching fader glides down following your finger. The big knob allows you to dim a whole room in one go or, with a press, connect to another room in your house. When you do that, the four faders slide into place to mirror that room’s lights. If you move a fader, your phone will reflect the change. And, if you put a thumb on a fader midslide, the motor simply gives up. “Your hand wins,” as the manufacturer puts it. Overengineered for Warp 9 nerd joy Each of the faders can run a single lamp or a group of lamps. You can also set them to change color temperature or even color instead of brightness, if your light can produce different hues. The four metal keys are for saved scenes, four per room. Oh, and if a light doesn’t dim, the fader goes into what Dufetel calls “snap mode”: it fights your thumb for a moment, then slams to the end of its travel, imitating the way a toggle does it. There’s no spring or detent inside. “The motor does all of it,” Dufetel tells me. As you push, the motor pushes back harder and harder, “then past a certain point it lets go and drives the fader the rest of the way, so it snaps over like a wall switch.” He tuned that feel by hand at his bench. [Photo: Sacrebleu] It doesn’t stop at lighting. You can use the knob as a volume dial for Sonos or any other speaker hooked up to Home Assistant. The 2.4-inch AMOLED screen reveals the track information, because of course it does. It’s small and mostly monochrome on purpose, though. “The screen isn’t meant to be the hero of the product,” Dufetel says. The F4 talks to the hub you probably already own, whether it’s Philips Hue, Lutron Caséta, or Home Assistant, the open-source platform that can run lights from Ikea, Lifx, Nanoleaf, and others. [Photo: Sacrebleu] Dufetel writes that the console grew out of “a nostalgia for old hi-fi gear: solid materials, and controls you could feel.” He tells me that, if he had to name one influence from the stereos he grew up with, he says, “it would be the old Marantz receivers, with their wood cases and aluminum controls.” The four faders come from Alps, a Japanese component maker, he says in his FAQ. The keys are NKK switches. According to the designer, the knob, key caps, and front panel are anodized aluminum cut from solid stock. The oiled walnut case comes out of his workshop near Seattle, its four sides mitered from a single plank “so the grain wraps around the corners,” he tells me. He designed it to stay on the table for decades. Sacrebleu is taking $50 refundable deposits on 100 units, with shipping beginning sometime after March 2027 to the U.S. and Canada for now (you can add your name to an international waiting list). It comes with a two-year warranty and a 30-day return window. My favorite thing about Dufetel’s physical gadget pitch is the last item in his FAQ: “Couldn’t I just use my phone to control my lights?” The answer is three words long: “Yes, you could.” Would Blofeld use a phone app to control his laser to kill Bond? Yeah. Exactly.

Recent findings suggest that somewhere inside a hollowed-out volcano, a bald man stroking a white cat is playing a Barry White LP and dimming down his lair’s halogens with the F4 lighting console. Or perhaps operating an orbital weapon. I want one. The control panel. The orbital weapon, too. Maybe a synthetic polar bear rug while we’re at it.

According to recent reports, designed and made by Sacrebleu, a one-person workshop in Washington state run by Alex Dufetel, the F4 is a home automation console that resembles a tiny audio mixing board. The 13 x 7.5 x 3.5-inch device has four motorized faders, a fat aluminum knob, four metal keys, and a small screen, all wrapped in walnut.

It costs $1,700. It does absolutely nothing my phone can’t already do, but who cares. I just can’t resist the ’70s vibes. And physical controls are just better. While manufacturers avoid them to save on costs, many people want them back. As Dufetel tells me, “Our hands want physical feedback: something to push against, and a response they can feel.”.

According to recent reports, dufetel used to run a Meta team working on how people interact with virtual and augmented reality (remember Zuck’s metaverse?). The F4 is 2,000% a much better use of his talent and time. Just look at the faders. They work like the motorized sliders on a massive recording studio desk. They move by themselves. If you dim your original 1962 Flos Arco lamp—because, if you have $1,700 to sink into a lighting console, you have an original Arco lamp—in your living room using your phone’s home automation app, the matching fader glides down following your finger.

The big knob allows you to dim a whole room in one go or, with a press, connect to another room in your house. When you do that, the four faders slide into place to mirror that room’s lights. If you move a fader, your phone will reflect the change. And, if you put a thumb on a fader midslide, the motor simply gives up. “Your hand wins,” as the company puts it.

Sources indicate that each of the faders can run a single lamp or a group of lamps. You can also set them to change color temperature or even color instead of brightness, if your light can produce different hues.

The four metal keys are for saved scenes, four per room.

Oh, and if a light doesn’t dim, the fader goes into what Dufetel calls “snap mode”: it fights your thumb for a moment, then slams to the end of its travel, imitating the way a toggle does it. There’s no spring or detent inside. “The motor does all of it,” Dufetel tells me. As you push, the motor pushes back harder and harder, “then past a certain point it lets go and drives the fader the rest of the way, so it snaps over like a wall switch.” He tuned that feel by hand at his bench.

It doesn’t stop at lighting. You can use the knob as a volume dial for Sonos or any other speaker hooked up to Home Assistant. The 2.4-inch AMOLED screen indicates the track information, because of course it does. It’s small and mostly monochrome on purpose, though. “The screen isn’t meant to be the hero of the product,” Dufetel states. The F4 talks to the hub you probably already own, whether it’s Philips Hue, Lutron Caséta, or Home Assistant, the open-source platform that can run lights from Ikea, Lifx, Nanoleaf, and others.

Dufetel writes that the console grew out of “a nostalgia for old hi-fi gear: solid materials, and controls you could feel.” He tells me that, if he had to name one influence from the stereos he grew up with, he says, “it would be the old Marantz receivers, with their wood cases and aluminum controls.” The four faders come from Alps, a Japanese component maker, he says in his FAQ. The keys are NKK switches. According to the designer, the knob, key caps, and front panel are anodized aluminum cut from solid stock. The oiled walnut case comes out of his workshop near Seattle, its four sides mitered from a single plank “so the grain wraps around the corners,” he tells me. He designed it to stay on the table for decades.

Sacrebleu is taking $50 refundable deposits on 100 units, with shipping beginning sometime after March 2027 to the U.S. and Canada for now (you can add your name to an international waiting list). It comes with a two-year warranty and a 30-day return window.

Recent findings suggest that my favorite thing about Dufetel’s physical gadget pitch is the last item in his FAQ: “Couldn’t I just use my phone to control my lights?” The answer is three words long: “Yes, you could.” Would Blofeld use a phone app to control his laser to kill Bond? Yeah. Exactly.

#115755. A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster

📅 07 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1540 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1540 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles.
  • But position and time are different.
  • Sources indicate that the discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles. Werner Heisenberg's famous uncertainty principle states that certain properties, such as a particle's position and momentum, cannot both be measured with unlimited precision. This restriction is not caused by flaws in scientific instruments. It is built into the laws of nature.

But position and time are different. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle does not impose the same restriction on these quantities. Now, researchers have experimentally demonstrated another fundamental limitation: an electron's location and its behavior over time cannot both be determined with arbitrary precision. Known as the "space-time limit," this newly observed relationship could have major implications for the future of quantum technology and ultrafast electronics.

Sources indicate that the discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs. Jascha Repp, Rupert Huber, Franz Giessibl, and Klaus Richter, along with a team at the Max Planck Institute in Hamburg led by Angel Rubio.

Watching Electrons Move at Incredible Speeds.

According to recent reports, understanding how matter behaves at the smallest scales is essential for developing the next generation of technology. Advances in clean energy, quantum computing, and powerful electronics for artificial intelligence all depend on knowing how chemical reactions unfold, how light interacts with materials, and how electrons travel through electronic devices.

However, even the sharpest microscopic photographs cannot reveal the full picture. Scientists also need to observe how these processes change over time, effectively creating slow-motion movies of events occurring at the atomic scale.

According to recent reports, at RUN, researchers are developing ultrafast microscopes capable of recording the movements of electrons, atoms, and molecules with extraordinary precision in both space and time. About ten years ago, scientists in Regensburg used ultrafast scanning tunneling microscopy to resolve the movement of a single molecule across space and time for the first time.

Tracking individual electrons presents an even greater challenge. At these microscopic distances, electrons can move roughly a thousand times faster than atoms and molecules, with vital changes taking place over just attoseconds.

To appreciate how extreme these scales are, consider that an atom is approximately ten million times smaller than a millimeter. An attosecond is one-billionth of a billionth of a second. The difference between an attosecond and a second is comparable to the difference between one second and the entire age of the universe.

Recent findings suggest that making these measurements is especially difficult because electrons do not behave like ordinary objects. Their motion follows the unusual laws of quantum mechanics rather than the familiar rules of classical physics.

Ultrafast Lasers Reveal Quantum Tunneling.

To observe electron behavior at these extraordinary speeds, the researchers built a latest laser system that provides much finer time resolution than earlier experiments. The system allows them to control and study the quantum motion of individual electrons directly.

In a recent development, in the experiments, carefully timed laser pulses drive electrons from an extremely sharp metal tip toward a silver surface. The distance they travel is only a few atomic diameters.

The researchers detect this movement by measuring the resulting electrical current. To determine exactly when the electrons move, they use two pulses of light separated by a precisely controlled interval.

Simon Maier, the lead author of the paper, explains: "By varying the time interval between the two laser pulses, we can directly observe how the electrons respond.".

Sources indicate that this approach revealed clear evidence of electron motion occurring on attosecond timescales. It indicated that the laser pulses could transfer electrons within these incredibly brief intervals while allowing scientists to observe the process as it happened.

Industry observers note that what makes the result particularly remarkable is how the electrons travel. Instead of moving like conventional particles, they behave as quantum waves. This allows them to pass through an energy barrier separating the metal tip from the silver surface, even though classical physics predicts they should not have enough energy to cross it.

This phenomenon, known as quantum tunneling, is somewhat like an object passing through a solid wall without breaking or damaging it.

"Our measurement can be understood as a high-speed camera for the electron wave packets, since you can see at what point in time the tunneling process takes place," explains Katharina Glöckl, a doctoral student and co-author of the publication.

A Surprising 500-Attosecond Delay.

Industry observers note that to understand the measurements more deeply, researchers working with Prof. Angel Rubio performed sophisticated quantum simulations of the electrons' behavior near the "space-time limit.".

It has been revealed that their calculations closely reproduced the experimental findings and uncovered another remarkable detail. The electrons did not respond to the light field instantaneously. Instead, their motion lagged behind it by approximately 500 attoseconds.

At such extreme scales, several fundamental features of quantum physics become important simultaneously.

It has been revealed that for example, the researchers found that the laser pulses could not be described entirely by treating light as a wave or entirely by treating it as individual particles called photons. Their effects displayed characteristics of both descriptions. This combination was essential for exploring electron behavior so close to the "space-time limit.".

The team also discovered that controlling electron motion over extremely short intervals changes how the electrons are distributed in space. Quantum mechanics describes these electrons using wave packets, which represent how their wave properties extend across different locations.

The relationship between the timing of electron motion and the spatial extent of these wave packets revealed the central limitation behind the discovery.

A Hidden Tradeoff Between Space and Time.

Raffael Spachtholz, another co-author of the study, explains: "The more precisely we want to pin down the electron's position in time, the more energy we need to provide. And as a result, the electron wave packet spreads out more spatially.".

In other words, improving the precision of an electron's timing comes with a cost. The more tightly researchers define when its motion occurs, the more broadly its quantum wave packet spreads through space.

To examine this relationship experimentally, the team placed a single atom on the surface to confine the electron wave packets to an extremely small region immediately before the laser pulses arrived.

This setup allowed the scientists to directly measure the connection between the electrons' spatial distribution and the timing of their motion.

Importantly, even when the electrons received substantial energy from the laser pulses, their wave packets remained sufficiently localized for microscopy with atomic spatial resolution and attosecond time resolution.

Industry observers note that the findings provide experimental insight into a fundamental space-time constraint that scientists had previously only suspected. They also make it possible to systematically investigate how changes in electron motion over time affect the spatial structure of quantum wave functions.

Could Quantum Electronics Become Hundreds of Thousands of Times Faster?

Beyond revealing a newly introduced aspect of quantum behavior, the discovery could open the door to technologies that operate on timescales far beyond the capabilities of today's electronics.

One especially promising possibility involves using precisely controlled electron wave packets to influence chemical reactions.

It has been revealed that transferring a single electron to a molecule represents the smallest possible transfer of electric charge. But when that electron is concentrated within an exceptionally small region of space and time, the resulting local peak current density can reach as much as 1 trillion amperes per square centimeter.

Such extreme conditions could give scientists newly introduced ways to control chemical bonds and observe how molecules change during reactions.

"In the future, we want to use such wave packets to specifically trigger chemical reactions and observe, on the relevant length and time scales, how chemical bonds can be broken or altered," explains Prof. Jascha Repp enthusiastically.

According to recent reports, the implications could extend well beyond chemistry. Greater control over electron motion may eventually help engineers develop electronic devices and quantum information systems that operate at speeds approaching the fundamental limits of electron dynamics.

"In the long term, the insights gained could also contribute to operating electronics and quantum information processing at the intrinsic speed limit of electron motion itself -- hundreds of thousands of times faster than the right now dominant CMOS technology," adds Prof. Rupert Huber.

Sources indicate that that possibility remains a long term technological goal rather than an achievement demonstrated in the current experiments. Nevertheless, the findings provide a new foundation for exploring how electrons can be manipulated at the smallest distances and shortest timescales.

According to recent reports, for Repp and Huber, the results suggest that the range of potential applications is extraordinarily broad. They believe that future advances in controlling electrons at the space-time limit may ultimately depend more on human creativity than on the constraints imposed by nature.

#115753. Black Friday is bad for the planet. These brands are opting out

Black Friday is bad for the planet. These brands are opting out

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2030 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Black Friday is an environmental disaster.
  • Recent findings suggest that researchers from the University of Leeds in the U.K.
  • The term “Black Friday” goes back to the 1950s, when the police in Philadelphia used the term for the chaos after Thanksgiving when suburban shoppers flooded the city.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Black Friday is an environmental disaster. Researchers from the University of Leeds in the U.K. found that up to 80% of items bought on that day, along with the plastic packaging they come in, end up in a landfill, incineration, or at best, low-quality recycling. All this after a very short time of use, sometimes as little as a few weeks. Shipping contributes to the damage; emissions from trucking spike 94% during the week including Black Friday. The term “Black Friday” goes back to the 1950s, when the police in Philadelphia used the term for the chaos after Thanksgiving when suburban shoppers flooded the city. In 1961, the city’s merchants tried and failed to rename it “Substantial Friday.” In the 1980s, the retail industry tried to reconceptualize it as the day that they go from being in the red to being in the black. Today, however, Black Friday is no longer a day. It’s an entire season stretching from late October to early December. And as a marketing ploy, it works well: Americans spent a record $11.8 billion online on Black Friday last year. The urgency of shopping these deals often leads to regret: 42% of shoppers in one survey conducted by Self Financial, a credit building manufacturer, said they wished they hadn’t made at least one Black Friday purchase. According to the National Retail Federation, retailers expect 17% of holiday sales to be returned, and roughly 9.5 billion pounds of returned merchandise goes into U.S. landfills every year. Opting out is bad for business. Black Friday weekend is one of the most lucrative stretches in the retail year, as consumers are primed to open their wallets. But a handful of brands is choosing to take a stand and abstain from sales. Here are brands that are confirmed to opt out on November 27. REI The outdoor co-op first chose to skip Black Friday in 2015 with its “Opt Outside” launch, starting a national conversation about Black Friday’s impact. And while the brand lost sales that Friday, it led to a major brand boost in the form of social impressions. In 2022, REI decided to make its store closure on the day permanent. All REI stores, distribution centers, call centers, and headquarters will be closed. Customers can still order online, and fulfillment resumes the next day. On its website, REI offers ideas for opting outside. Instead of shopping, it encourages customers to go on a hike, a neighborhood walk, or a picnic in the park. That sure sounds more pleasant than endlessly refreshing social media for new deals. Patagonia Patagonia declared war on Black Friday in 2011 when it took out a full-page New York Times ad telling people “Don’t buy this jacket.” This year, it has no Black Friday sale. It has a Black Friday microsite that pokes fun at the false sense of urgency the day often entails. It says that its emphasis on creating high quality gear “is an unlimited time deal that has nothing to do with Black Friday or Cyber Monday. Honestly, the best jacket is the one you already own.” Its website remains open on Black Friday, but there is no sale. Instead, the brand encourages you to shop its secondhand “Worn Wear” collection. In a radical move Patagonia recently put its secondhand products alongside its new products on its website. And if you do choose to buy something new, it encourages you to buy products that will last a lifetime, and offers care and repair guides. More importantly, it lays out ways to give back, including its network of grassroots environmental nonprofits. The Ordinary (Deciem) When Deciem first went dark on Black Friday in 2019, it called the closure “a moment of nothingness” and encouraged customers to “buy less, but better.” On November 27, the websites for all of Deciem’s brands—The Ordinary, Niod, Loopha and The Chemistry Brand—will be closed, as will its standalone stores. Instead, it will transform stores, including those in New York and Toronto, into sites for a blood drive. In its London and Copenhagen stores, it will invite customers to identify their blood type, so they can be equipped to participate in other blood drives. Lush Lush doesn’t run Black Friday sales. The company says its prices reflect the true cost of its ingredients, such as the organic Peruvian jojoba oil in its Gorgeous moisturizer. Instead, it has long used the day for activism. In 2016, it “switched off” its websites around the world on Black Friday, drawing people’s attention to the nonprofit Access Now. In 2021, it chose Black Friday to announce that it was quitting a number of social media channels; Mark Constantine, the CEO, said he was “happy to lose” $13 million. In the U.K., Lush stores will be using the Black Friday and Cyber Monday period to raise money through Charity Pot, a lotion that funds grassroots groups. Freitag The Zurich bag maker, which launched in 1993 creating bags from old truck tarps, has been saying no to Black Friday since 2019, encouraging customers: “Don’t shop, just swap.” Since then, its online store has been closed every Black Friday, and visitors are redirected to S.W.A.P. (Shopping Without Any Payment), its bag exchange platform. Over the years, Freitag has offered fun swap events at its stores. The company hasn’t announced its 2026 plans yet, but it’s a good bet that it won’t be running a Black Friday sale. Veja The French sneaker brand hasn’t held a Black Friday sale since 2017 and apart from its outlets, it doesn’t offer any discounts. Instead, it has turned the day into “Repair Friday.” In 2024, it invited people to its Paris headquarters to have things repaired by experts for free, from shoes and clothing to furniture, computers, and phones. In 2025, every Veja cobbler offered two hours of free repairs, and anyone could drop off one pair of sneakers from any brand. (Veja provides shoe repair in nine stores in Europe, North and South America.) Veja hasn’t announced its 2026 plans yet.

Is Kling 4.0 the Right AI Video Generator for Your Project?

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

According to recent reports, weekly. Free. One click to leave.

In a recent development, 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Recent findings suggest that A short clip can help a project in different ways. It can show an idea you have not filmed, put an existing design in motion, or give an announcement something to look at. The same approach will not work if the clip needs to demonstrate a real feature or show exactly what happened. Before choosing a generator, decide what the viewer needs to learn from the shot.

This article uses Kling 4.0 as a worked example, but the decision process applies to any AI video generator. It covers how these tools turn prompts and images into video, how Kling 4.0 and a few alternatives differ, how to choose a starting mode, how to add exact text and branding outside the generated clip with a short ffmpeg script, and when real footage is the better choice. Feature details come from each vendor’s own pages at the time of writing and change often, so confirm current terms before you blueprint a production.

Sources indicate that ● Generated video is best for imagined shots. It suits concepts, backgrounds and early explorations, not instructions or faithful records.

● Your starting material decides the mode. A written idea, a reference image or a pair of opening and closing frames each call for a different input.

In a recent development, ● Keep exact wording out of the generated clip. Titles, dates and logos belong on separate layers in an editor.

Recent findings suggest that ● Tools differ on control, cost and licensing. Compare inputs, length, resolution, credits and terms before you commit.

● Always review. Watch the whole clip at its final size and check it against the real product or design.

Most current systems extend diffusion models across time. A model learns to turn noise into a coherent set of frames guided by a prompt, and sometimes by an image or a clip. The research paper Video Diffusion Models describes this extension from images to video. The practical consequences are easy to observe.

According to recent reports, ● The prompt describes change over time. One visible change and one camera instruction usually work better than a long list of actions.

Recent findings suggest that ● Reference material steers but does not lock. A picture can suggest shape and colour without guaranteeing an exact match.

It has been revealed that ● Longer clips give more room for drift. Faces, logos and fine text are the first things to change between frames.

Industry observers note that ● Cost grows with length and resolution. Most hosted tools charge credits per second, so short previews are cheaper than full shots.

In a recent development, if you only have an idea, start with text. For a short announcement, you might ask for a band of light to move across a wall of coloured tiles. No one needs to recognise a particular wall, so the model can decide how it looks. Give it one visible change and a clear view of the subject. A prompt such as Soft morning light travels slowly across a wall of blue ceramic tiles. Fixed camera, no lettering is enough to see whether the idea works.

Sources indicate that if you already have an illustration or a photo, reference mode gives you another starting point. Suppose you want a short concept clip for a desk accessory that only exists as a drawing. The picture can show the general shape and colour while the prompt describes the view you want. A video reference can help when it is the motion that is hard to explain, such as a slow camera slide. Say what each asset is meant to guide, and do not add a clip just because you have one.

Industry observers note that use keyframes when a particular view matters at a particular moment. Start with an opening image. If a short reveal also needs to end with the object facing forward, add an ending image to show that view. That is different from a reference image that mainly shows what the object looks like. Neither method guarantees an exact match, so check the result rather than assuming the uploaded picture has locked the design.

In a recent development, no single tool fits every project. The table summarizes what each option’s own page states, and “not stated” means the page did not say, not that the feature is absent.

Reading the table: hosted studios such as the one on JXP are the quickest way to test an idea and need no setup, but you pay per second and work within their supported inputs. Kling’s own site is the place to check announcements and API options directly, since its page says little about durations or resolution. Runway positions its models for motion quality and prompt following, while Google’s Gemini API video documentation suits teams building generation into their own products. The Diffusers video guide covers open-source pipelines for developers who want local control and are ready to manage GPUs and licences.

According to recent reports, trying an idea before making it. An illustrator might want to see how an imagined landscape feels when the light changes. A quick clip gives the team something to discuss: is the change visible, and does it happen at the right pace? It does not need to be the final animation to answer those questions.

Showing a product concept. A rotating view or a slow camera move can help people discuss how a design might be presented. It is useful early, when the shape and lighting are still being explored. Once the clip represents a product someone can buy, the standard changes. If a port moves or a button appears that the real product does not have, it is the wrong clip for that job.

According to recent reports, making a short visual for a post. A few seconds of moving colour can give an event announcement or a project update a distinctive opening. Put the name, date and other exact wording in your editor so they are readable and easy to change. The background only needs to support the message. If it competes with the text, use less movement or keep the background still.

It has been revealed that generated video is unreliable at lettering, so add titles in an editor or with a script. The command below overlays a title on a generated background and then checks the file properties. It assumes you already have a clip named background.mp4 and ffmpeg installed.

-vf "drawtext=text='Launch Night | 12 March':fontcolor=white:fontsize=64:x=(w-text_w)/2:y=(h-text_h)/2:box=1:boxcolor=black@0.35:boxborderw=24" \.

-c:v libx264 -pix_fmt yuv420p -an announcement.mp4.

ffprobe -v error -select_streams v:0 \.

-show_entries stream=width,height,r_frame_rate,duration \.

-of default=noprint_wrappers=1 announcement.mp4.

Industry observers note that because the text lives in the command, you can reuse the same background for three events by changing one string. The font may need to be set with a fontfile option on some systems. This is the practical version of keeping the moving background in one file and the editable details in another.

If people will follow the clip as instructions, use real footage or a screen recording for the steps. A convincing shot of an app is not proof that a button is in the right place. A generated close-up of a product is not a reliable way to show how its parts fit. You can still use an imagined opening, but make the switch to the real demonstration clear.

According to recent reports, think about revisions, too. If your team expects to adjust the same title, logo or date every week, put those elements on separate layers in an editor. And if the only movement you need is a slow zoom on an approved picture, apply that zoom directly. There is no reason to risk changing the picture when a simple edit will do.

This matters when someone else will maintain the video. A reusable announcement template is easier to hand over if the moving background is one file and the event details are editable. If the team likes the movement but needs three versions with different dates, they can reuse the same clip. If every change calls for a latest generation, the time you saved on the first version may disappear on the second.

The Kling 4.0 video generator on JXP presently offers 720p and 1080p settings and clip lengths from 3 to 30 seconds. According to its page, reference mode accepts up to 10 images and 5 videos, keyframe mode takes a first frame, middle frames and an optional last frame, and credits are charged per second with a higher rate at 1080p. For a first attempt, choose the frame shape you plan to use and make the clip only as long as it needs to be. Check the displayed credit cost before generating, because a short preview can tell you whether the direction works before you spend on a longer shot.

Recent findings suggest that decide what a good result looks like before you generate it. For the tile background, you need to see the light move without distracting from the words you will add. For a product concept, check whether the shape stays recognisable as the viewpoint changes. Watch the whole clip at the size the audience will see it. If the shot misses the point, revise one thing at a time: the motion, the framing or the source image.

According to recent reports, ● Read the licence. JXP’s page lists a commercial use license on each blueprint and claims outputs are for creative and lawful use, with the user responsible for reviewing them. Other tools have different terms.

According to recent reports, ● Do not misrepresent products or events. A generated clip should not suggest features or footage that do not exist.

● Consider provenance. C2PA is an open standard for Content Credentials that records where content came from and how it was edited, and some tools support it.

● Disclose where required. Follow platform and advertising rules on labelling AI-generated or altered content.

● Fine text, logos, hands and fast motion can drift or flicker between frames.

● Reference images and keyframes steer the result but do not guarantee an exact match.

● Vendor specifications, such as resolution and length, can differ between a model announcement and a particular platform.

● Credit costs and blueprint terms change, so check them on the day you generate.

● Long or exact sequences are often cheaper and safer to film than to generate.

Short imagined shots, concept clips and moving backgrounds, where some details can be left open and the clip is reviewed before use.

Use text when you only have an idea, reference mode when you have a picture or clip to guide the look, and keyframes when specific views matter at specific moments.

Recent findings suggest that not reliably. Use real footage or a screen recording for instructions and demonstrations.

Industry observers note that no. Hosted studios, vendor sites, developer APIs and open-source pipelines all exist. Compare supported inputs, length, resolution, cost and licensing against your project.

Industry observers note that kling 4.0 is a good candidate when the missing piece is an imagined shot and you can describe what it needs to do. Pick one such shot, try it, and put it next to the material you already have, and compare at least one alternative before you commit. If the project needs exact instructions or a faithful record, use the real thing. A useful first result is one that does its job in the edit, not simply one that looks impressive on its own.

Tech Report: GrapheneOS highlights off how it intends RCS support without Google Messages

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (301 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • RCS is coming to GrapheneOS without Google Messages, as a proof-of-concept app demonstrates how the privacy-focused version Android can implement the messaging standard.
  • Industry observers note that as virtually all Android phones and now iPhone support RCS messaging, the standard is key to communication in 2026.
  • It’s a problem that Graphene’s developers have been trying to work out for a while now, and it seems progress is being made.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

RCS is coming to GrapheneOS without Google Messages, as a proof-of-concept app demonstrates how the privacy-focused version Android can implement the messaging standard.

Industry observers note that as virtually all Android phones and now iPhone support RCS messaging, the standard is key to communication in 2026. But GrapheneOS users, by default, are still stuck with SMS/MMS as RCS is typically locked behind Google Messages on Android.

It’s a problem that Graphene’s developers have been trying to work out for a while now, and it seems progress is being made. A proof-of-concept messaging app with RCS was shared on Twitter/X, showing Graphene’s RCS implementation working with both Google Messages and iOS with end-to-end encryption and full features including typing indicators and reactions.

While this app skips the need to use Google Messages directly, the app does still use Google’s services as most carriers rely on Google for RCS. GrapheneOS still needs a sandboxed version of Google Play, for now, for this to work, but the developers say that a standalone version for carriers that support Google-less RCS will be coming.

It has been revealed that we made a proof of concept RCS messaging app. It already has end-to-end encryption with MLS compatible with Google Messages and iOS, typing indicators, delivery/read receipts, reactions and media/file sharing. We'll use what was learned to integrate RCS into our Messaging app. pic.twitter.com/jzCTCCKrIQ.

There’s still no firm timeline for this fresh RCS support on GrapheneOS, but Google Messages can still be used in the meantime.

#115750. Industry News: The state of China's memory industry in 2026

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2813 w)

Industry News: The state of China's memory industry in 2026

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2813 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, china’s homegrown memory comes largely from two companies, CXMT for DRAM and YMTC for 3D NAND, and both are booming.
  • Sources indicate that both are expanding and adding fabs, and each is edging into the other’s products.
  • Memory is a commodity, so the story is in the wafers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, china’s homegrown memory comes largely from two companies, CXMT for DRAM and YMTC for 3D NAND, and both are booming. CXMT’s Oct. 30 quarterly report shows a nine-month net profit of ¥132.0 billion ($19.6 billion), against a ¥5.28 billion ($785 million) loss a year earlier, on revenue more than eight times as high, at ¥269.0 billion ($40.0 billion). YMTC’s numbers, just for Q1, are at ¥47.04 billion ($7.0 billion) in revenue and ¥33.38 billion ($5.0 billion) in profit attributable to shareholders, more than double 2025.

Sources indicate that both are expanding and adding fabs, and each is edging into the other’s products. No Chinese manufacturer can yet produce high-bandwidth memory (HBM) in volume, though. HBM is the stacked DRAM that AI accelerators depend on, and currently the U.S. bars Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron from selling it into China. CXMT’s prospectus lists no HBM project, though its HBM3E is reportedly in risk production, an early run before the process is fully qualified. Huawei designs its own HBM but doesn’t say who makes it.

Memory is a commodity, so the story is in the wafers. We cover the companies running memory fabs in China: CXMT, YMTC, a handful of smaller Chinese fabs, and Samsung and SK hynix, which run some of their biggest plants there. Huawei makes the cut for its HBM program, though it has no memory fab. Fabless designers, module makers, and NOR flash producers are left out, except XMC for its HBM line. Fab counts, products, and financials come from filings and company statements; capacities, planned fabs, and the HBM progress that remains the substantial question mark rest largely on anonymous reporting. Let's dive into the current state of the Chinese DRAM industry.

CXMT, short for ChangXin Memory Technologies, is China’s biggest homegrown DRAM maker. It operates two 12-inch fabs in Hefei and one in Beijing, each able to produce around 100,000 wafers a month. It is also building fabs in Shanghai and Hefei and is in funding talks for a second Beijing fab, which together could take it past 600,000 wafers a month. The Shanghai fab is expected to have two to three times the capacity of the Hefei base, with tools going in during the second half of 2026 and volume in 2027.

It has been revealed that CXMT is now the fourth-largest DRAM maker worldwide, with 9.5% of DRAM revenue in Q2, according to TrendForce. CXMT says LPDDR6 is in mass production for Xiaomi, and its president says the first 4F² product, a server DDR5 RDIMM, is due by year-end. This comes after record first-half revenue of ¥150.3 billion ($22.4 billion), net profit of ¥77.6 billion ($11.5 billion), an 84.84% gross margin on its main business, and a listing on Shanghai’s STAR Market on July 27. Third-quarter profit alone was ¥54.4 billion ($8.1 billion).

The primary products are DDR5 rated up to 8,000 MT/s with 24Gb dies, and LPDDR5X rated up to 10,667 MT/s. CXMT states its fifth-generation G5 platform reaches 11.95nm active-area half-pitch with quadruple patterning for 24Gb LPDDR5X, and gets at least 50% more dies out of each wafer than G4, counted as 8Gb dies. CXMT says a DRAM product on its sixth-generation platform has also completed engineering-sample validation. Jeongdong Choe, Senior Technology Fellow at TechInsights, told Tom’s Hardware Premium that the firm measured the smallest active half-pitch on CXMT’s G4 at 14.8nm and hasn’t analyzed G5 yet.

Industry observers note that CXMT lists no GDDR or 3D NAND among its products and is limited to nodes made without extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography as it lacks the tooling. CXMT’s second Beijing fab, however, is planned to include a 3D NAND R&D line, which could shake things up. The growth picture for now is capacity and price, with the tests of scaling without EUV lying with the RDIMM and Shanghai fab.

According to recent reports, YMTC, short for Yangtze Memory Technologies Co., has two fabs of its own in Wuhan, which can produce about 200,000 wafers a month together. A third fab in the Xinzhou district, registered in September last year, is expected to produce about 50,000 wafers a month by 2027 and eventually 100,000 at full capacity. While YMTC is known for its NAND flash, roughly half of Fab 3’s output is earmarked for DRAM. The company also makes enterprise SSDs and UFS and eMMC parts, and sells consumer SSDs under its ZhiTai brand. YMTC filed its own STAR Market prospectus, to match CXMT’s, on Aug. 21.

In a recent development, NAND flash was, until recently, the star of the show for Chinese memory, and YMTC’s Xtacking technology is one reason why. Its fifth-generation Xtacking 4.0 die, used in 1Tb TLC and 2Tb QLC parts, has 294 gates, and Choe told us 267 of them are active word lines. Most of what YMTC ships, however, is still 160- and 232-layer NAND. Samsung licensed YMTC’s Xtacking bonding patents in February 2025, so the technology could be considered both proven and valuable.

Omdia data put YMTC at 38.5% of China’s NAND market in Q2, ahead of Samsung’s 33.5%. Globally, YMTC ranked third in NAND shipments in Q2, according to Counterpoint Research, and its share of NAND revenue rose from 9% to 14% between Q1 2025 and Q1 2026. YMTC’s stated long-term targets are about 20% of global NAND supply and about 500,000 wafers a month, DRAM included.

Industry observers note that for DRAM, YMTC’s Fab 2 is running about 5,000 wafers a month of 16Gb LPDDR5, still in R&D and testing, with no plan for mass production. However, a 9,600 MT/s part on a vertical channel transistor (VCT) 4F² cell is slated for mass production at Fab 3 if it passes qualification. XMC, YMTC’s former foundry unit, left its control in July.

It has been revealed that two smaller fabs worthy of note are Fujian Jinhua and SwaySure. The former has a 12-inch fab in Jinjiang, which produces custom DDR4 on 25nm, at 40,000–50,000 wafers a month, with about 90% going to Huawei. DDR4 prices have surged this year, by as much as 50% in the first quarter alone, as the big suppliers wind DDR4 down in favor of server and HBM parts and enterprise buyers stock up.

SwaySure, a Shenzhen firm founded in March 2022 with state-owned investment, is building a 28nm 12-inch DRAM line and is reportedly backed by Huawei. Analyst Jim Handy of Objective Analysis doubts the 28nm line could make HBM. Neither company responded to our requests for additional information.

Hefei Phase 1 and Phase 2 (Anhui); Beijing (Yizhuang).
