According to recent reports, not every AI chip needs HBM. Inference hardware can get by on LPDDR5X, as Axera’s AX8860P does in Sipeed’s MaixStation, or on DRAM bonded straight onto the processor, the approach PieceMakers is betting on. Training-class accelerators like Huawei’s Ascend series still need HBM, though, and since the U.S. banned the export of HBM as of Dec. 2, 2024, China can’t buy it from the substantial three memory makers.

Recent findings suggest that even those who can get HBM are seeing heat and yield challenges with larger memory stacks, specifically 12-high. SK hynix remarked on its Q3 2026 earnings call that some customers’ spec changes show “demand is indeed overwhelming supply,” and that lowering the stack is “a strategy to increase the number of cubes that can be obtained for the same capacity.” This mirrors other indicators, including potential Nvidia Rubin Ultra decisions, and it suggests that HBM is in short enough supply that even easier-to-build stacks are in high demand.

CXMT has sampled HBM with Tongfu, and HBM3 built on its 16nm-class G4 node to Huawei. Its HBM3E has now gone to several domestic AI chip designers as samples, with limited production due by the end of 2026, and an expansion expected in 2027. Yields are only about 20% to 30%, though, against about 70% at SK hynix, and in testing the chips performed closer to SK hynix’s HBM3 than to its HBM3E. An HBM packaging plant in Shanghai worth at least ¥17.1 billion ($2.5 billion) is targeted for year-end, with capacity for about 30,000 units a month.

Tongfu reportedly sampled HBM2, but its own filings mention only DRAM and flash packaging. Huawei said last year that “we will offer two proprietary HBMs.” It launched the Atlas 350 card in March, built on the Ascend 950PR, which carries 112GB of HBM. XMC has had a 3,000-wafer-a-month HBM line under construction since early 2024, but no production has been confirmed. At this time, YMTC, Jinhua, and SwaySure don’t appear to make HBM, though reports say YMTC is developing the through-silicon via (TSV) stacking it would need, and Jinhua was named in a Huawei-led HBM group in 2024.

It has been revealed that huawei remarked in 2025 that the 950PR would use HiBL 1.0, its own “low-cost HBM”; TechInsights told us it hasn’t analyzed HiBL 1.0 yet. However, Huawei’s 2025 roadmap specced out the 950PR's 128GB of HBM at 1.6TB/s. Huawei said that its 950PR is “optimized for the prefill stage of inference,” which is compute-heavy with “lower demand for memory access bandwidth,” and that using HiBL 1.0 is “more cost-effective than HBM3E and HBM4E” for that workload. The higher-end HiZQ 2.0, for the 950DT, is due in Q4 and, by Huawei’s figures, brings 144GB at 4TB/s. In both cases, Huawei’s supplier remains in doubt, and the organization did not respond to our requests for comment.

HBM3 samples to Huawei; HBM3E sampling, with limited production by year-end at 20–30% yields.

Under construction; due by the end of 2026.

Of the companies from outside China, Samsung and SK hynix both run large memory fabs on Chinese soil, and both are now upgrading their NAND lines there. Samsung’s Xi’an handles about 40% of the tech giant’s NAND, including 236-layer, or V8, in volume, with X2 converting to 286-layer, or V9, this year, slated to reach 5,000 V9 wafers a month in December and 40,000 by December 2027. A Samsung spokesperson told Tom’s Hardware Premium that the company “has been transitioning its existing manufacturing operations in Xi’an to 9th-generation V-NAND in compliance with U.S. export regulations and in close communication with the U.S. government.”.

SK hynix’s Wuxi produces 30–40% of its DRAM and has moved from 1z to 1a, with the EUV layers done in Korea. Dalian turns out about 100,000 wafers a month of 192-layer floating-gate NAND and is moving to 240 layers, the most SK hynix is authorized to make there.

It has been revealed that SK hynix, which already sells NAND with up to 321 layers elsewhere, told us it needs a U.S. license every year and declined to give product details or capacities for individual fabs. The tech giant mentioned that it intends for its 321-layer flash to be “over 50% of domestic (Korean) capacity in the fourth quarter,” which puts the Dalian lag into relief.

SK hynix also has “Mod B,” a second fab at its Dalian site that was completed in 2023. The firm has reportedly tied a new U.S. NAND fab to Washington, letting it ship more U.S. tools there: Dalian’s 2026 license capped its equipment, no 2027 license had been issued as of mid-October, and its U.S.-based Solidigm unit has applied for an export license to buy more tools for Mod B. SK hynix told Tom’s Hardware that “no capacity expansion is being sought for the Dalian Mod B” and has been installing equipment at its Dalian factory.

Sources indicate that solidigm is now reportedly in talks with the U.S. Commerce Department over a $45 billion chip plant in the U.S., but wants Washington’s approval to ship equipment to upgrade the Dalian plant first, arguing that the upgrade would help finance the newly introduced site. However, SK hynix denied an earlier report of such a deal and says no specific plans have been finalized.

Recent findings suggest that as for its Chongqing packaging plant, SK hynix told us it is “exploring various strategic options to enhance our packaging competitiveness,” though nothing is final. Elsewhere in China, Samsung’s Suzhou plant handles assembly and testing, and Micron’s Xi’an site handles packaging and testing.

It has been revealed that all of this plays out inside a U.S.-China fight over chips that AI has only sped up. CXMT isn’t currently on the Commerce Department’s Entity List, which bars U.S. suppliers from shipping to listed companies without a license; YMTC, Jinhua, and SwaySure are. Jinhua has been on the list since 2018; SwaySure joined in December 2024 over its Huawei links, and YMTC was added in December 2022.

CXMT is, however, on the Pentagon’s 1260H list of Chinese military companies, which it is suing over. It’s been on the list since January 2025 and stayed on with the June upgrade. For Samsung and SK hynix, the validated end-user status that let both firms ship in U.S. tools was revoked as of Dec. 31, 2025. Annual licenses are now required, and the Commerce Department has said it doesn’t intend to license capacity expansions or technology upgrades. Meanwhile, both companies say upgrades are under way, which sits uneasily with that policy.

Sources indicate that china, for its part, has been weighing broader technology export controls and has now proposed adding 40 technologies, reportedly including some memory-chip design technologies, to its Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited and Restricted from Export. The draft, Announcement 48 from China’s Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Science and Technology, is open for comment until Nov. 15, and anyone exporting a listed technology must register first.

3D NAND: 236-layer V8; V6 ended.

About 40% of Samsung’s NAND (both Xi’an fabs).

3D NAND, converting to 286-layer V9.

Converting to V9; 5,000 V9 wafers a month in December 2026, 40,000 by December 2027.

DRAM, mostly 1a; EUV layers done in Korea.

Floating-gate 3D NAND, 192-layer, moving to 240.

About 100,000 wafers a month; 30% to 40% of SK hynix’s NAND.

Producing; upgrading, authorized up to 240 layers.

Built in 2023; SK hynix says no expansion is sought; no 2027 license yet.

According to recent reports, presently, China’s homegrown memory hinges on two manufacturers that are, admittedly, booming at the moment, although the memory industry worldwide has seen a massive surge since spring 2025. SK hynix remarked that “our DRAM and HBM volume for the next three years through 2029 are effectively sold out” with supply failing to keep up with demand as “a constraint projected to continue through 2030.” Its average selling prices rose from Q2 by mid-20% for NAND and high-20% for DRAM.

There may be some signs of at least temporary cooling in China’s consumer channel, though, as China Flash Market reports that SSD prices fell across the board this week, with most spot NAND wafers trading more than 30% below suppliers’ official prices. It looks like supply will remain a hot topic and China’s production capabilities are front and center.

CXMT and Huawei both have HBM milestones due by year-end: CXMT’s limited HBM3E production and Shanghai packaging plant, and Huawei’s 950DT with HiZQ 2.0. YMTC’s Fab 3 is due in late 2026 or 2027, and CXMT’s HBM3E expansion is expected in 2027. That leaves little time to ramp within 2027, especially at CXMT’s current yields, so we’re skeptical of volume HBM from a Chinese fab, whether measured against domestic demand or global supply, before 2028. Samsung and SK hynix, meanwhile, still need U.S. licenses for next year to keep tooling their Chinese fabs.

Shane Downing is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware, covering consumer storage, PC hardware, and AI.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Maybe we just don’t talk about AI this Thanksgiving. Of course, we need some common conversation topics to throw around the dining room with friends and relatives we haven’t seen in a while. And though AI seems to be showing up everywhere now, we still have a lot of other stuff to talk about—sports, food, movies, and the like. Or there’s always that thing where you go around the table and everybody says something they’re thankful for. Unless somebody actually says “Claude” (which is fine). Mostly there are good reasons to avoid the subject of AI at your gathering this year. Too political. Talking politics in mixed company at the Thanksgiving table can have unpredictable, sometimes explosive results. AI has become very political, mainly because of AI data centers. A surprising number of midterm voters cited an aversion to latest AI data centers as the main rationale for their swing toward Democrats. Studies have shown that data centers do indeed contribute to rising energy costs, not to mention the noise pollution they produce. In fact, data centers are already so prevalent that there’s a decent chance one of your Thanksgiving guests lives near one. (You may recognize them by the way they keep saying, “Huh? What? Huh?”) Sore subject. Too technical. The last major tech wave, mobile computing, was pretty easy to conceptualize. They turned cellphones into internet devices with major screens and made computer programs called apps to run on them. AI is different. Very few laypeople can explain how a neural network is trained and how it operates. Even PhDs don’t know exactly how AI models develop new skills, some of which have come as a complete surprise. That creates a problem for Thanksgiving conversation. Somebody at the table who listens to a lot of podcasts may seize the moment to nerd-splain AI to everybody. Or worse, they may go on and on about how LLMs are just stochastic parrots—word-guessing machines that will never be capable of anything more. Pedantry, jargon, and boredom will waft through the air around the table. With luck, the speaker will take the blank stares looking back at him as a signal to put a turkey leg in his mouth. Too painful. Somebody at the table might own a bunch of Nvidia or SpaceX stock and get depressed. Or somebody might remind everybody that their retirement accounts are already bound up in risky AI-dependent stocks like SpaceX. Someone may gaze up from their stuffing with a faraway look and recall those simpler times when Jensen Huang was a one-woman man and everybody believed that all the AI companies buying up Nvidia GPUs would actually be able to pay for them, with nary a revenue stream to match. Heady days! They are over. Nvidia has lost 20% of its value this year because maybe bankrolling your profit-free customers the cash to buy your product isn’t the most sustainable business plan. So just don’t bring it up; heavy drinking may ensue. Too personal. Don’t ask people what they use AI for. It can lead to some bad places. Just last year, a 22-year-old sitting across the table from me began talking about all the personal stuff she discussed with ChatGPT. I promptly tuned her out, of course, but there was something in there about an antifungal cream, a GLP-1 “crisis,” and a neurodivergent ex-boyfriend. Too anxiety-inducing. Somebody in the house Thursday may have that soon-to-be-unemployed vibe about them, and it’s quite possible that an AI has already learned to do their job. Challenger, Gray & Christmas found that AI was the top-stated reason for U.S. job cuts through October. Soon that person will be spending their days in the uncanny valley, doing video interviews with wooden-faced AI avatars, only to be passed over (and over) by a candidate-screening algorithm that was offended by their Zoom background. On a more serious, and more anxious, note, whether people realize it or not, our relationship with AI is pretty different from what it was at this time last year. The models aren’t perfect, or even trustworthy in some applications, but they’ve clearly become more intelligent. We hear about teams of AI agents working tirelessly on big problems, coding agents building entire apps, and models solving some of the world’s hardest math problems. We may be headed for a world where we coexist with coequal, nonbiological intelligences that are generally as smart as humans. Discussing where this is all headed can make for an uncomfortable conversation, and not one suitable for a holiday gathering. I’d leave it be this Thanksgiving. Turkey legs and existential angst just aren’t a good mix. The trouble is, AI has seeped into everything, raising the constant question: How is AI affecting this? So you must listen closely for signs of conversational drift toward the AI thing and have some safe, go-to topics ready to throw in. Like these: Remember the World Cup this summer? Wasn’t that nice? For the first time in a while, I felt a tinge of real national pride as I watched the crowds of foreign football fans having a ball alongside Americans in our cities and stadiums. Americans got rave reviews for their hospitality—everybody from Uber drivers to hotel staff to strangers who helped our international guests get around. My favorites were those videos of Europeans discovering the simple joy of chicken tenders, pizza, and french fries slathered in ranch dressing. Returning to the moon. In April, NASA’s Artemis II mission sent a crew of astronauts on a loop around the moon, taking them 252,756 miles from Earth—farther than any humans had ever traveled. They spotted a crater on the lunar surface and named it after the crew commander’s late wife, Carroll. The return of the jaguar. A jaguar nicknamed “Cinco” is roaming southern Arizona’s mountains, only the fifth jaguar seen there since monitoring began 15 years ago. Researchers say it’s the latest sign that the endangered species may be gaining a foothold in the region. They also say that Cinco has a distinctive mark on its face that resembles Groucho Marx’s mustache. Beating cancer. For the first time, 70% of Americans diagnosed with cancer survive at least five years, the American Cancer Society says. In the mid-1970s, only half did. Fewer overdose deaths. U.S. overdose deaths fell about 14% in 2025, the third straight annual drop and the longest decline in decades, according to provisional data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. And finally, Costco’s hot dog and soda combo still costs $1.50, the same as it did in 1985. You can thank me later. Happy Thanksgiving.

Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1136 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection.
  • Sources indicate that unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing.
  • In a recent development, by harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection. Physicist Yiwen Chu and her team have developed a system that uses microscopic mechanical vibrations to store and manipulate quantum information, much like the vibrating strings of a guitar produce musical notes.

Sources indicate that unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing. They take place within a tiny quantum chip, where they serve as a new form of computer memory.

In a recent development, by harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory. "The interaction between the quantum processor and the quantum memory provides a crucial foundation with a view to establishing quantum computers as a powerful and reliable way to perform computations that are not feasible with conventional computers," says Yiwen Chu.

The breakthrough, described in the journal Science, introduces a different approach to quantum computer design. Instead of closely integrating information processing and storage, as many existing systems do, Chu's team has developed an architecture that gives these functions more distinct roles.

Quantum Memory Inspired by Conventional Computers.

The researchers drew inspiration from the basic design of everyday digital computers. In a conventional machine, the central processing unit (CPU) carries out calculations while information is held separately in working memory, commonly called random access memory (RAM). The arrangement of these components plays an important role in determining how efficiently a computer operates.

In a recent development, chu's quantum system follows a similar principle. A superconducting qubit acts as the processing and control unit, performing a role comparable to that of the central processing unit (CPU). Meanwhile, a separate quantum memory temporarily holds the information needed during calculations, allowing the processor to retrieve and modify it as necessary.

The major difference lies in how that information is stored.

"In our quantum working memory, however, information is not stored electromagnetically -- as is usually the case today -- but rather in the form of mechanical vibrations," explains Chu.

Quantum computers take advantage of unusual properties of quantum physics, including superposition, which allows quantum systems to exist in combinations of different states, and entanglement, which creates powerful connections between quantum states. These effects could eventually enable quantum machines to tackle certain extremely complicated calculations much faster than conventional computers, including some problems that are currently beyond their practical capabilities.

Why Vibrating Quantum Memory Could Be Better.

According to recent reports, one of the greatest challenges in quantum computing is maintaining precise control over quantum information. The states used for calculations are delicate, and even small disturbances can cause information to be lost. To perform calculations reliably, the processor and memory must interact closely enough to transfer and manipulate quantum states with high precision.

Recent findings suggest that in the newly introduced system, microscopic structures called mechanical resonators hold information in particular patterns of vibration. When the superconducting qubit needs that information, it accesses the stored vibrational state, performs the required operation, and returns the modified information to memory.

Many existing quantum computers instead use electromagnetic memory alongside superconducting qubits. Researchers understand these technologies well, and they can be combined to provide extremely accurate control over quantum states, including reading, changing, and manipulating stored information.

However, electromagnetic memory systems have a significant disadvantage. They can occupy considerable space, making it difficult to expand experimental quantum devices into the larger, more capable computers that researchers and industries ultimately need.

Mechanical resonators offer several potential advantages. They are substantially smaller, allowing more compact designs. They can also support numerous different patterns of vibration, providing opportunities to store more information simultaneously than conventional electromagnetic memory.

Another crucial benefit is that mechanical vibrations can preserve quantum states for longer periods before the stored information begins to fade. Longer storage times could make it easier to carry out complicated calculations that require information to remain available throughout multiple processing steps.

New Quantum Computer Passes Major Tests.

Recent findings suggest that the research published in Science provides the first experimental demonstration that mechanical resonators can work together with superconducting qubits to carry out quantum computations. The results establish that vibration-based memory is a feasible alternative to electromagnetic storage.

The achievement goes beyond simply storing information. Chu's team demonstrated that its architecture can handle both relatively straightforward calculations and more demanding quantum operations.

Recent findings suggest that to evaluate the system, the researchers tested two important computational techniques: the quantum Fourier transform and period finding. Both are fundamental tools in quantum computing and require a computer to coordinate multiple quantum states with considerable precision.

Industry observers note that "The Quantum Fourier Transform is a fundamental computational procedure required for many quantum algorithms. The period-finding algorithm we implemented served as a demonstration of how this procedure can be used," explains Igor Kladaric, doctoral student in Chu's team and co-author of the publication.

Successfully completing these tasks requires the system to store, control, and maintain coherent relationships among multiple quantum states at the same time. The experiments revealed that the fresh architecture can meet these requirements, providing strong evidence that it can support genuine quantum computation rather than simply function as a memory device.

A Promising Step Toward Powerful Quantum Computers.

It has been revealed that one of the most significant findings is that the upcoming system can, in principle, carry out all the fundamental operations needed for arbitrary quantum computations. This means the architecture has the essential capabilities required for a programmable, general-purpose quantum computer.

However, demonstrating those capabilities in an experimental chip is only the beginning. The next major challenge is scaling the technology to larger systems with greater processing power while preserving the precision and reliability demonstrated in the laboratory.

It has been revealed that chu and her colleagues are continuing to investigate how their approach can be developed further. Its long-term success will depend on whether mechanical quantum memory can remain effective as more components and increasingly complex computations are added.

Practical quantum computers powerful enough for widespread scientific and industrial applications are still some distance away. Nevertheless, by showing that tiny mechanical vibrations can serve as compact, capable quantum memory, the ETH Zurich team has demonstrated a promising new route toward making those machines a reality.

#115747. Tech Report: The surprising — and fun — way brands are AI-proofing themselves

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1678 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: The surprising — and fun — way brands are AI-proofing themselves

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1678 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that play is becoming the route to making truly creative, human work.
  • It has been revealed that play is becoming the route to making truly creative, human work.
  • Externally, that impulse is showing up everywhere.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that play is becoming the route to making truly creative, human work. As AI makes polished output cheap, abundant, and instantaneous, brands are increasingly looking to offer expressions of character, and ways to stand apart from the inevitable homogenization of content and communications. Externally, that impulse is showing up everywhere. Brands are lifting the lid on the creative process through behind-the-scenes content, embracing deliberately handmade visual expression and even using “No AI” disclaimers, like recent campaigns from Apple or Aerie.Each is an attempt to signal the presence of human thought and distinguish meaningful creative work from the flood of so-called slop. Internally too, creativity is the priority. A Marketing Week study in 2025 found that almost two-thirds of brand marketers had increased their focus on creative quality, while 63.9% rated it among the more influential factors in marketing effectiveness. Yet striving for more creativity is not the same as knowing how to enable it. Brand managers are often asked to protect consistency, reduce risk, and deliver at speed. Briefs are often loaded with history, data, and preconceptions; teams are rewarded for control; often, ideas are filtered out before they have room to develop. And the idea of true creativity can be abstract, intimidating, and unattainable. Play might sound unserious in that environment. But in fact, it can be a working method, helpful and inspiring; permission to experiment and make unexpected connections, combined with the expertise to select and execute the right idea. Unlocking its commercial advantage requires leaders to rethink how they brief teams, frame creativity, and manage brands. Here’s how to get started. Make room to play Original thinking needs guardrails, but also room to grow. A strong brief should get teams to the point where they can begin exploring, not overwhelm them with years of history and layers of data. The best chief marketing officers or brand managers get it. They do the research in advance, then set out the ambition for the brand with a suggested set of parameters and say “go and play’”(as Chris Willingham, CMO at Brompton Bicycle, did in our recent work together), offering clarity and trust to create the conditions for better work. This also makes the notion of creativity less obscure or intimidating. “Get creative” can feel like a loose and impossibly lofty instruction. “Go and play” is an invitation to explore. It shifts the focus from finding the right answer immediately to following ideas and seeing where they lead. The wrong idea can still reveal the right solution; rejected routes also clarify what a brand is not. Play demystifies creativity without lowering the standard. One time, a workwear manufacturer client challenged us to create something that looked deliberately “not right.” It was the perfect invitation to play, and resulted in a design that felt structured and familiar but punctuated by unusual interactions. Play to consumer intelligence Alongside a change in language needs to come an appreciation of a changing consumer and their needs. Brand consistency once offered reassurance. But today, the consumer expects their brands to be more animated, dynamic, nimble and responsive to the times we’re living in. Like people, brands can—and should—have different facets. Reliable in one moment, spontaneous or surprising in another. Wise, the money transfer platform, is a great example of a brand getting that balance right; the experience feels trustworthy, but also conversational, quirky, and human. Interactions with Wise are like talking to my intelligent, funny friend. It is an experience miles ahead of what banks like Barclays offer. It also reveals how crucial the notion of play is in the expressions of a brand—visual, verbal, behavioral. A brand doesn’t need to be irreverent or rebellious to embrace play. You can be one of the most serious companies but still allow playful elements of your brand to convey trust, accessibility or a more human approach. The connectivity provider rSIM, for example, offers a serious B2B product to healthcare, banking, and other utilities. But its brand and articulation are full of vim and vigor. It turns up with a unique character in a very technical field. Embrace the unexpected A more playful mindset also allows you to make unexpected connections, to produce the leap that makes an idea distinctive. Take the International Olympic Committee’s multiyear licensing agreement with Sonic the Hedgehog. Is it consistent with the famously strict Olympic brand guidelines? Debatable. But would Pierre de Coubertin, founder of the modern Olympic Games, approve? Absolutely. It’s a contemporary articulation of the Olympic ideal, which is to bring the youth of the world together in peaceful competition—and Sonic is a way to connect with young people around the world. Strategic play can uncover those connections, giving established purpose a fresh and culturally relevant expression. But it will always go hand in hand with judgment. The point is not about endless play or ideation. The commercial advantage comes from combining freedom with craft, self-editing, and the confidence to stop when the right idea appears.

…if you explore an idea in the Gemini app, AI Mode will have that foundation to build on, and vice versa.

Recent findings suggest that this builds on the existing ability to have the Gemini app factor your Search history into answers. With this upgrade, AI Mode can access “your Gemini chats, what you’ve shared with Gemini Apps (like photos, files, audio or video attachments, and screens you ask about), and associated insights and locations.” The option to make the connection is available today, but the feature will go live in the coming weeks.

You can control Personal Intelligence in AI Mode from this page.

Google will soon show a “Personalization” icon below tailored responses that lets you “view the context AI Mode uses.”.

The final update today will make AI Overviews and AI Mode responses “more personally relevant.”.

In a recent development, so if you’ve been researching and planning for a trip, you can pick up right where you left off in a newly introduced search thread without starting over or repeating yourself. As always, you can adjust or turn off personalization at any time in your Search Settings.

TouchTunes just added a social feed to your local jukebox

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2724 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The streaming jukebox giant TouchTunes wants to be the online social hub for your local bar.
  • The streaming jukebox giant TouchTunes wants to be the online social hub for your local bar.
  • In a recent development, the Newly introduced York-based manufacturer boasts jukeboxes in more than 60,000 locations that customers can control through touch screens or apps on their own smartphones.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The streaming jukebox giant TouchTunes wants to be the online social hub for your local bar. The New York-based organization boasts jukeboxes in more than 60,000 locations that people can control through touch screens or apps on their own smartphones. Now, it has added a “social feed” that lets users of its apps communicate with each other and see who’s connected to the jukebox in a particular establishment, even when they’re not physically there. App users can add comments and emoji-style reactions to recently played songs or share their own text posts, photos, and GIFs to a shared feed for a particular bar, restaurant, or other site with a TouchTunes jukebox. “We’re trying to transform from just the jukebox company to being the center of in-person social entertainment, and this is the natural next step of that,” says Scott Levine, the TouchTunes CEO. The company envisions that in addition to complimenting—or teasing—whoever’s playing the current song on the jukebox, users could visit a location’s feed for other discussions relevant to that spot, like planning to watch a game, recruiting players for a darts league, or sharing photos of a memorable night out. While Levine acknowledges TouchTunes is unlikely to replace existing group chats, and it’s not intended to compete with general-purpose social media apps, he anticipates the feed helping break the ice between fans of a particular venue and serving as a hub for good-natured discussions of what goes on there. “Maybe you have a smaller list or group of people—you’re going to communicate using message, or WhatsApp, or whatever,” he says. “But then when you’re there, you’re going to post a photo and your buddy that’s not there [will say] ‘oh man, I wish I was there.’”  Already, the company sees reactions being posted roughly every 15 seconds, and Wednesday, when young people traditionally return to their hometown bars the night before Thanksgiving, will likely make for a test of the new features. TouchTunes celebrates Thanksgiving Eve as National Jukebox Day, and Levine says it’s among the company’s biggest sales days, at least on par with St. Patrick’s Day. When jukebox fans first use the TouchTunes app to connect to a jukebox after the social feed is enabled, a pop-up message discloses the new feature and invites users to visit the app’s settings menu, where privacy options include opting out of having their usernames visible in the list of people at a venue and the list of songs being played. That’s intended to make sure that users feel in control of their privacy options, even if that leads to making themselves less visible, Levine says. “We bring you right to the screen to toggle it off,” he says. [Image: TouchTunes] But privacy experts question whether users will make informed decisions about what they’re sharing, particularly if they simply tap through the pop-up to access the normal jukebox menu, potentially while distracted—or intoxicated—in a busy bar. “I think a lot of times people are going to be at a bar, and they want a song being played,” says Sara Geoghegan, director of the consumer privacy program and senior counsel at the Electronic Privacy Information Center. “That is not the scenario that is best suited or most apt to understand your data and how it’s being used.”  Privacy concerns may naturally be greater for certain groups, like domestic violence survivors or immigrants, she says. They may also arise if someone encounters a creepy person at a bar who can use TouchTunes to figure out when they return or where they head next. In general, she says, tech companies rolling out new features can help mitigate concerns by ensuring that settings default to those maximizing privacy. “If they had the default [as] that privacy-protective option, we would have all of the benefits of the social media feed, and bringing people together, and having people enjoy music together in a shared space without the privacy concerns,” says Geoghegan. Still, Levine emphasizes that users can adjust their privacy settings—and block particular TouchTunes users from seeing information about them—whenever they choose. They can also report inappropriate posts that appear on particular venues’ feeds, similar to the options from other social media companies, and change their displayed usernames at any time. “We’re giving privacy controls on every single thing, and we’re trying to remind users, ‘Hey, you have control,’” he says. “And if you don’t like what somebody’s talking about, you can block them.”  Some TouchTunes users appear to use usernames derived from their real names or screen names they also use on other services. But others use what appear to be anonymous strings of words or characters that would make it difficult for strangers to identify them and link them to their lives outside the jukebox. “The first line of defense is to choose something like, I don’t know, HappySquirrel23,” says Jelena Mirkovic, a principal scientist at the University of Southern California Information Sciences Institute and research associate professor at USC’s Department of Computer Science who has studied privacy issues in social and payment apps. “And so now no one knows it’s me, but I can still use the app and have full functionality.”  In general, she says, app developers can help by considering privacy trade-offs, like whether information about someone’s location should be visible publicly or only to friends, and prompting users to reevaluate their privacy settings over time once they’ve become familiar with an app’s features. “Then you know people have a way to act on that, and that would be informed consenting at that time,” she says. Since the TouchTunes social feature is still new, it’s likely too early to say how jukebox fans and the bars and restaurants that serve them will use it in practice, versus sticking to existing social and location-sharing platforms. Levine envisions the company releasing additional tools to make it easy for venues to communicate with customers, such as publicizing specials or events, and leaderboards that could reward users who play crowd-pleasing songs as determined by reactions and likes. TouchTunes is also testing a feature that would let users dedicate a song to another user, or to a location at large, he says. Already, the TouchTunes app allows users to customize their profiles; they can add a brief bio and profile photo, select their favorite music genres, and even specify what they’re looking for, from “new tunes” and “pool players” to a “drinking buddy” or a “relationship.” Future versions of the app may include the ability to add other users as friends and potentially receive relevant notifications, says Levine. “If my buddies are all going out to the pizza restaurant down the street, and I want to go play a song for them because I know they’re there, I’ll be able to do that and join in,” he says. While cynics might argue TouchTunes is building digital infrastructure for conversations bar-goers used to have in person—such as when gathered around old school, physical jukeboxes with coins or dollar bills in hand—Levine argues the app can indeed help bring people together within venues, to applaud each other’s selections or offer to buy a round for someone playing fun songs. “They’re using their phones to do it, but it’s not about living in the phone,” says Levine. The app can also potentially let people participate in the community at a particular spot even if they’re not present, spotting photos of their friends at a particular bar, figuring out where to grab a meal or drink, or even playing a song from afar. Even before the social feed introduced, Levine says he heard from a business associate who used the app to pick bars to visit, looking for venues where jukeboxes had a long queue of songs, since they were likely to be lively. The feed will only make it easier for music fans to find venues that match their wants and needs and play the jukebox once they get there, he says. “Users win, a location wins, TouchTunes wins,” he says. “It’s this nice, simple, synergistic triangle.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Streaming in 1080p will be the default in Google Meet, regardless of whether you pay for Google Workspace. That includes personal Google Accounts.

According to recent reports, google says owners will default to sending and receiving 1080p video, at the minimum. Previously, Google Meet made 720p the standard for streaming, and a higher resolution had historically been locked behind the Google One 2TB initiative. That’s been true since 1080p streaming was rolled out in 2023.

The upgrade will roll out to everyone, including those with Google Workspace accounts and personal Google Accounts. The only requirement to stream your own 1080p video in Google Meet for web will be hardware-based. Google’s press release states that devices with cameras capable of streaming in high definition will do so, and the feature will be turned on automatically.

In a recent development, it can be disabled, though. Users can head to Settings > Video in Google Meet for web. Video will also appear in a lower resolution if the user’s video tile is shrunk down on-screen.

The upgrade appears to be centered on web-only instances of Google Meet, and might not include the app on Android or iOS. For the time being, those versions may still be limited to streaming in 720p for those who don’t have an active Google One subscription.

Google Meet started its extended rollout of 1080p streaming to everyone earlier this month, so it shouldn’t be much longer until the change has taken place completely.

Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1179 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A latest computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors.
  • It has been revealed that the approach has already revealed newly introduced candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications.
  • One of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A latest computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors. Developed by a researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL), the method makes it much easier to identify promising materials for quantum technology, potentially opening the door to advances across many areas of science.

It has been revealed that the approach has already revealed newly introduced candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications. The findings were recently published in ACS Central Science and have attracted attention from other researchers in the field.

One of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions. Many candidates require extremely low temperatures to function reliably. Diamond materials stand out because certain quantum properties can remain useful even at room temperature.

This capability could help advance technologies that are important to national research priorities and the development of next-generation computing. Quantum sensors promise levels of sensitivity and precision beyond those of conventional instruments, while quantum computers could eventually solve certain extraordinarily complex problems much faster than today's most powerful supercomputers.

Why Imperfect Diamonds Could Be the Key to Quantum Computing.

Although diamonds are made of carbon atoms, a flawless diamond crystal is not enough to create a useful quantum computing system. The key lies in tiny irregularities within the crystal structure.

Industry observers note that these imperfections, known as defects, can occur when a carbon atom is absent from its normal position, when another element replaces a carbon atom, or when both changes occur together. The atoms surrounding these defects can form qubits, the basic units used to store and process quantum information in quantum computers and sensors.

Sources indicate that finding the most useful defects, however, has been difficult. Accurately modeling their quantum behavior traditionally requires enormous computational resources, making it challenging to evaluate large numbers of possible candidates.

A Simpler Way to Discover Better Diamond Qubits.

Mark Martirez, a staff research scientist at PPPL, developed a way to dramatically reduce the complexity of these calculations. Instead of simulating a much larger diamond structure, he isolates a small region containing just 16 to 30 atoms around a defect.

By "carving out" this tiny atomic cluster and treating it like a separate molecule, Martirez can use powerful computational methods that chemists have spent decades refining. These established techniques make it possible to analyze the quantum properties of diamond defects much more efficiently without sacrificing the high level of accuracy needed for the calculations.

Industry observers note that "Because we're treating the qubits as molecules, the cost of calculating these defects is equivalent to the cost of just modeling a simple molecule," Martirez said. "This method really opened the floodgates" in terms of how qubits can be assessed.

The new technique allows researchers to calculate how different qubits respond to laser light and microwave pulses far more rapidly than before. Using this approach, the team identified promising defects involving boron and oxygen that could serve as new types of qubits.

Fresh Diamond Defects Reveal a Spectrum of Quantum Colors.

According to recent reports, light plays an important role in how scientists interact with diamond qubits. Researchers use lasers and microwave pulses to manipulate their quantum states and retrieve stored information.

Recent findings suggest that much of the previous work in this area has centered on a defect known as the nitrogen-vacancy center. This structure forms when a nitrogen atom takes the place of a carbon atom in a diamond crystal, while an adjacent position that would normally contain another carbon atom remains empty.

Under laser illumination, this type of defect can emit red light when it occupies a particular quantum state.

According to recent reports, the newly investigated defects offer different optical properties. Oxygen defects can produce blue light, while those involving boron emit ultraviolet light.

These differences could make it possible to combine several types of qubits within a single quantum device. Because each type responds differently to light, researchers might be able to interact with one group of qubits without disturbing another.

"One could imagine, then, combining different qubits of different responses, so you can basically probe one qubit but not the other," Martirez said.

According to recent reports, beyond identifying new candidates, the findings suggest a broader change in how researchers approach quantum technology. Diamond qubits have traditionally been studied primarily through physics, but understanding their underlying chemistry could provide additional ways to design them.

Martirez believes that researchers could eventually engineer qubits for particular functions using principles similar to those applied when chemists create specialized molecules, including compounds designed for new medications.

How Quantum Chemistry Could Transform Future Research.

The potential benefits extend well beyond the development of quantum computers themselves. Martirez sees an intriguing possibility in which advances made possible by quantum chemistry eventually lead to quantum technologies that help improve the field of chemistry.

In other words, quantum chemistry could develop the very tools needed to "enrich itself" in the coming decades.

It has been revealed that A practical quantum system containing multiple qubits could make molecular calculations substantially more accurate. That would allow scientists to study increasingly complex chemical structures, including large biological molecules and proteins, with a level of detail that is difficult to achieve using conventional methods.

"We could describe larger molecules, biomolecules, proteins and everything like that in a more accurate way, and that could improve all the chemical-adjacent industries, such as pharmaceutical science and materials science. Even our fundamental understanding of molecular systems could be enriched.".

Such improvements could have far-reaching implications for pharmaceutical development, materials research, and the fundamental study of how molecules behave.

In a recent development, martirez also hopes the research will encourage more chemists to explore solid-state physics. Although building advanced quantum computers is often viewed as a challenge primarily for physicists, he argues that chemistry offers valuable expertise that could help accelerate progress.

"At this moment in time, there's a great emphasis on building the first state-of-the-art qubit computer," he noted. "But it's not just physicists who should be participating in this research. Chemists have decades of developed intuition about chemical systems that could be easily translated into understanding defects in solids as well.".

By bringing these disciplines together, scientists may be able to develop more effective ways to discover, understand, and eventually engineer the quantum materials needed for future technologies.

The research was funded through PPPL's Laboratory Directed Research and Development program under prime contract number DE-AC02-09CH11466, with additional support from the DOE Office of Science, Office of Fusion Energy Sciences.

Alice Huang has been accused of being a Chinese spy, and her affair with Jensen Huang saw the Nvidia founder resign. But even with Jensen Huang now back in the saddle at Nvidia, attention has turned to whether she posed, or poses, a security threat to the United States as a whole, and its place in the global AI food chain. A Upcoming York Times report details the meeting for staff members of the House and Senate intelligence committees and aides to the leaders of both chambers, including its bombshell news that Alice Huang's husband has a much more significant intelligence connection.

It has been revealed that the intelligence officials told those in attendance that they still don't fully understand what role Alice Huang played in the saga, but that there is no evidence that she initiated the affair at the behest of Chinese authorities. That being noted, they also refused to dispute that she passed intelligence back to the country's top intelligence agency while the affair was underway. Further, the officials told those at the meeting that Alice Huang's husband, Kang Wei, was a more significant figure with respect to any connection to the MSS. In fact, he had at times been an MSS asset with deeper contacts within the agency than his wife. It's been reported that Alice Huang was in contact with the Chinese spy agency from the spring of 2025 until the fall of 2026, while Kang Wei was also in contact with the same agency during that time.

Alice Huang was a Megaspeed employee when it was a customer of Nvidia. The data center organization was buying Nvidia's AI chips and is now under a criminal investigation over claims that it was bypassing export controls in an effort to get those advanced chips into China. The company has since been placed on a U.S. blocklist.

Trump later pressured Nvidia to rehire him, going so far as to call into a board meeting to do so. Despite Trump's backing, Jensen Huang must still face Congressional and Senate committees to discuss Nvidia, export controls, and any national security threats brought about by his infidelity.

#115741. Why isn’t AI changing career advice?

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1715 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

Why isn’t AI changing career advice?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1715 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ask a 17-year-old where their career strategy came from and the answer is usually someone at the kitchen table.
  • Sources indicate that ask a 17-year-old where their career proposal came from and the answer is usually someone at the kitchen table.
  • The school counselor rarely enters the picture.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ask a 17-year-old where their career strategy came from and the answer is usually someone at the kitchen table. A parent, maybe an uncle. These are people who love them and want the best for them. They are also, in most cases, working from a job market map that is 20 or 30 years out of date. The school counselor rarely enters the picture. Most U.S. school counselors spend no more than 20% of their time on career counseling while serving hundreds of students. The available capacity works out to well under an hour per student per year, even before accounting for group programming and administrative responsibilities. Meanwhile, nearly the entire AI and jobs conversation is about what this technology will take away from young workers. That concern is fair. I’ve argued here before that AI will reduce the need for some entry-level white-collar roles, and employers need to plan for that now. But we have become so focused on what AI will do to young workers that we have stopped asking what it can do for them. And there is an irony sitting right in front of us. One of the hardest problems in workforce development is getting accurate, real-time labor market information to the people who need it most. That happens to be the kind of problem AI is unusually good at. THE DATA EXISTS BUT FEW CAN READ IT Labor market data is not scarce. Governments, job boards, and industry groups publish enormous amounts of it every month. The trouble is that it is dense, scattered, and close to illegible for anyone without a statistics background. A 16-year-old is not going to read a state workforce projection. Neither is her dad. So young people make one of the biggest decisions of their lives with the least information. We are preparing them for yesterday’s jobs while tomorrow’s technology sits on the phone in their pocket. They know the system is failing them. In the Broken Marketplace, a Schultz Family Foundation and HarrisX survey of more than 5,700 young Americans ages 16 to 24, more than four in 10 mentioned the education system and the employment resources available to them are broken. Seven in 10 said they learn about career pathways on social media. We know that young people are already asking algorithms for career advice. They are just asking the wrong ones. WHAT A GOOD AI COUNSELOR SOUNDS LIKE At the International Youth Foundation, we’ve been testing this idea with a chatbot called Clara, a partnership we have with the Salesforce Foundation. Industry News: Driving for Thanksgiving? These are the worst times to be on the road this week

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1134 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Another Thanksgiving week is upon us, which means tens of millions of Americans will once again travel by plane, train, and automobile to see their loved ones.
  • Sources indicate that another Thanksgiving week is upon us, which means tens of millions of Americans will once again travel by plane, train, and automobile to see their loved ones.
  • “After three years of record highs, the number of travelers is slightly lower partly because of higher travel costs this year,” indicates Stacey Barber, vice president of AAA travel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Another Thanksgiving week is upon us, which means tens of millions of Americans will once again travel by plane, train, and automobile to see their loved ones. However, this Thanksgiving period will be a little different than in recent years—at least when it comes to transportation. That’s because the American Automobile Association (AAA) indicates that, for the first time in several years, fewer Americans will be traveling. “After three years of record highs, the number of travelers is slightly lower partly because of higher travel costs this year,” says Stacey Barber, vice president of AAA travel. “But travelers won’t notice much of a difference on the roads and at the airports, since projected volumes remain near record levels.”  That means that despite fewer travelers, the roads are still expected to be packed at times. With that in mind, here are the best and worst times to travel by car over the 2026 Thanksgiving period. Best times to hit the roads for the Thanksgiving travel period For the 2026 Thanksgiving period, AAA expects 72.9 million people to travel to their holiday destinations by car. That’s down from last year’s 73.1 million automobile travelers, but still a significant amount. AAA defines the 2026 Thanksgiving period as the seven days lasting from Tuesday, November 24 to Monday, November 30, 2026. But despite the expected 72.9 million road travelers, how congested the streets will be depends heavily on when you travel during the period. AAA says these are the best times to be on the road (ie: the times with the expected lowest congestion) over the period, according to transportation data and insights provider INRIX data compiled by the auto organization: Tuesday, November 24: Before 1:00 PM Wednesday, November 25: Before 12:00 PM  Thursday, November 26 (Thanksgiving): Minimal Traffic Impact Expected  Friday, November 27: Before 12:00 PM  Saturday, November 28: Before 11:00 AM  Sunday, November 29: Before 11:00 AM  Monday, November 30: Before 1:00 PM  Worst times to hit the roads for the Thanksgiving travel period INRIX data indicates that the worst days to travel over the Thanksgiving period—that is, the days the congestion is expected to be the highest—are the Tuesday and Wednesday before Thanksgiving, and the Sunday and Monday after. Those are the days when most people choose to travel to and from their holiday destinations. As for the individual times that are expected to be the worst to travel by car, those are: Tuesday, November 24: 2:00 PM to 8:00 PM  Wednesday, November 25: 12:00 PM to 7:00 PM  Thursday, November 26 (Thanksgiving): Minimal Traffic Impact Expected  Friday, November 27: 1:00 PM to 7:00 PM  Saturday, November 28: 12:00 PM to 9:00 PM  Sunday, November 29: 12:00 PM to 8:00 PM  Monday, November 30: 2:00 PM to 7:00 PM  Fewer total travelers are expected over the Thanksgiving 2026 period When combining all modes of transportation—auto, air, and “other,” which includes bus, boat, and train—AAA says 81.48 million people in America are expected to travel over the 2026 Thanksgiving period. That’s about 121,000 fewer than the 81.61 million who traveled during the 2025 Thanksgiving period. Still, 2026’s expected numbers far surpass the 77.78 million people who traveled in 2019, the last year before the pandemic. The expected decline in travelers this year is mainly due to higher travel costs, especially gas prices, AAA says. Besides a decline of about 200,000 car travelers, AAA says there will also be a drop in air travelers by about 0.2% to 5.96 million (versus 5.97 million in 2025). However, more people will travel by “other” modes during this period than last year. “Other” includes travel by bus, train, and cruise. In the 2026 Thanksgiving period, the other travel segment is expected to reach 2.6 million travelers—up 4.1% from 2.49 million in 2025.

In a recent development, AI companions are the most demanding consumer use of large language models right now. A coding assistant can forget your last message and still be useful. A companion that forgets your name, your running story, or the strategy you made last Tuesday has failed at its one job. On top of that, users now expect voice calls that feel like a phone conversation, not a walkie-talkie exchange with a five-second pause.

Three engineering problems decide whether a companion app works: how much of the conversation fits in the model's context window, what the app remembers once the window fills up, and how fast the voice pipeline answers. Here is how consumer companions handle each one, with real tier and pricing examples, and what developers can take from their designs for their own products.

Recent findings suggest that most LLM products are judged on single answers. Companions are judged on continuity. That creates pressure in three places at once:.

Every consumer companion is a different set of trade-offs across those three constraints, and the trade-offs are increasingly how the apps are priced.

Industry observers note that the context window is the total number of tokens the model can see when it writes the next reply. In a companion app, that budget is spent before the user says anything:.

Recent findings suggest that when the chat log outgrows what is left, the oldest messages fall out. The user experiences this as the companion "forgetting" mid-conversation. This is why context size is now a headline spec in the category, and a paid feature. SpicyChat AI, for example, gives free accounts a 4K context window, then scales memory to 8K on its $19.95/mo tier and 32K on its $29.95/mo tier. Janitor AI runs about 9K of context on its own JanitorLLM. Independent uncensored AI chat benchmarks record these context sizes alongside refusal behavior and pricing, because context length predicts how long a roleplay stays coherent better than any marketing claim.

Some apps sell memory in messages rather than tokens. Fantasy GF's pricing page lists a 60-message base "smart memory" and 5x that, 300 messages, on its Ultra plan. Others sell it as a memory multiplier on higher subscription tiers. The pattern is consistent across the category: memory depth is the upgrade lever, not the model itself.

Sources indicate that no consumer app keeps an entire relationship in the prompt. Persistent memory is a separate system that writes to storage and reads back into the context window on each turn. In practice it has three layers:.

It has been revealed that the differences users notice are usually retention policies, not algorithms. Crushon AI's own subscription docs say free-strategy chat history is deleted after 7 days of inactivity, while paid plans keep it for the membership period. Paid tiers across the category commonly promise that memories never expire. There is also a security angle worth stating plainly: companion chat logs are among the most sensitive data a consumer product can hold. A 2024 breach at Muah.ai, first reported by 404 Media, exposed roughly 1.9 million users' email addresses together with their private prompts. Any app that builds persistent memory is also building a liability, and developers copying the pattern should treat the memory store as the most protected part of the system.

It has been revealed that A voice call in a companion app is three models chained together: speech-to-text, the LLM, and text-to-speech. Run them strictly in sequence and a single reply can take several seconds, which reads as dead air. The apps that feel fast attack each stage the same way:.

With every stage streaming, time-to-first-audio can land close to a second on a good connection, which is roughly the threshold where a conversation stops feeling laggy. Voice is also expensive to run - three model calls instead of one, plus audio bandwidth - which is why it is metered harder than text. Fantasy GF charges 8 tokens per minute for voice calls (4 on Ultra), which turns the 100 monthly tokens on its entry plan into about 12 minutes of call time. SpicyChat, for its part, only adds text-to-speech at its top tier. Latency engineering and unit economics are the same problem here: faster pipelines cost less per call, and cheaper calls are what make voice viable below the top plan.

Tier details below come from each app's own pricing or documentation pages, checked November 16, 2026, and cross-checked against il.ly's AI companion testing guide, which hands-tests 15 companion apps across memory, media, and voice.

Industry observers note that two takeaways from the table. First, nobody sells a bigger base model - they sell a bigger window into the same one. Second, the free tiers are deliberately memory-poor: limited context and short retention are the upgrade prompt.

Even if you never build a companion, these apps are a useful reference architecture for any stateful LLM product:.

Consumer AI companions have turned three hard infrastructure problems - bounded context, durable memory, and real-time voice - into their pricing pages. Context size, memory depth, and voice access are the tiers. If you are building anything stateful on an LLM, this category is worth watching closely: it is solving continuity and latency problems at consumer scale, in public, one subscription tier at a time.

Industry observers note that it is the total amount of text, measured in tokens, that the model can consider when writing its next reply. The character definition, stored memories, recent chat, and the newly introduced message all share that budget. When the conversation exceeds it, the oldest content drops out and the companion appears to forget.

Recent findings suggest that yes, through a memory system separate from the context window. Apps summarize older chats, extract stable facts about you into a profile, and retrieve relevant past moments into the prompt. Retention varies: some free tiers delete chat history after as little as 7 days of inactivity, while paid plans typically keep memory for the membership period.

It has been revealed that A voice turn runs three models - speech-to-text, the LLM, and text-to-speech - instead of one, plus audio transfer. Providers pass that cost on through per-minute token charges or by locking voice behind higher tiers.

For casual chat, 4K to 9K tokens works. For long-running roleplay or a companion expected to hold plot threads for weeks, 32K and up, or a well-built memory layer on top of a smaller window, makes the visible difference.

Despite some huge setbacks, VR gaming is still alive and well, popping out tons of amazing games this year that you may not have realized. Throughout the entire festival, you can expect tons of newly introduced game demos on Steam, including over 220 games from nearly 150 developers. While the festival is technically on Steam, Meta Quest still rules the roost in the VR world, so you can expect plenty of surprises for Quest gamers.

This year’s judges include Zeena Al-Obaidi (CCO at VR Games Showcase), Ian Hamilton (Founder of Good Virtual Reality), Naysy (Content Creator, VR Forever Ambassador), and Nicholas Sutrich (me!).

In a recent development, the full list of winners and nominees will be unveiled during the show, but Creature highlights Forefront, Thief VR: Legacy of Shadow, Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Empire City, Dungeons of Eternity, Titan Isles, and the ever-popular Hot Dogs, Horseshoes & Hand Grenades 2 as some of the most notable. Visit the VR Forever website to learn more, and check out Naysy’s video above for even more details!

#115736. Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism

Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (456 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Googleblog

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, long-context training — including pretraining and post-training, has become a foundation of frontier AI models.
  • In particular, efficient training at multi-million-token sequence lengths runs into the following bottlenecks:.
  • Sources indicate that today, we are excited to announce long-context training support in MaxText, Google Cloud's open-source JAX training framework.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, long-context training — including pretraining and post-training, has become a foundation of frontier AI models. Longer native sequence lengths give large language models (LLMs) the working memory to read a whole code repository or ingest hours of video, and reason through multi-step agentic tasks. In three years, context windows have grown from 128K–200K tokens to 1M–2M, and models trained toward 10M tokens are arriving. Training at those lengths, not just serving them, is where the system limits show up.

In particular, efficient training at multi-million-token sequence lengths runs into the following bottlenecks:.

Sources indicate that today, we are excited to announce long-context training support in MaxText, Google Cloud's open-source JAX training framework. MaxText enables this by supporting four context-parallel strategies on Cloud TPU: All-gather, A2A (DeepSpeed Ulysses), P2P (Ring Attention), and the A2A + P2P hybrid (Unified Sequence Parallelism, or USP), combined with load balancing and sequence packing. All four use the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel. Combined with the 3D inter-chip interconnect (ICI) ( supported on TPUs such as TPU 5p or TPU 7 (Ironwood) ), this lets one sequence span an entire slice while communication overlaps compute and memory per chip stays flat. In our benchmarks, Llama 3.1 8B (25 head dim, 16 query heads) demonstrates exceptional long-context efficiency, achieving 70% Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) on TPU 5p for sequence lengths up to 4 million tokens. Across both TPU 5p and TPU 7, context can be seamlessly extended to 14 million tokens—with TPU 7 consistently maintaining 50% MFU across all sequence scales below 6 million tokens.

This functionality is available today in MaxText v0.2.4(doc).

Context parallelism splits a long sequence across chips, so no chip holds the activations of the whole sequence. Context parallelism can be combined with data and tensor parallelism, and the smallest context-parallel size that fits your sequence in HBM is usually the right one. This also holds for sparser attention variants which cut attention compute but not the activations of every other layer.

It has been revealed that attention is the one global operation where every token needs the keys and values of every preceding token, so each context parallel strategy has to bring those keys and values back together. Each makes a different tradeoff between memory (how much KV a chip holds), communication (how much moves per layer, and whether it overlaps compute), and model shape (how many attention heads to split).

Industry observers note that all-gather: Each chip keeps its chunk of the sequence and, at every layer, gathers the keys and values from every other chip. It is the simplest option. However, because causal masking causes later tokens to attend to larger prefixes, All-gather requires balancing compute load across devices.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, evan Reece has a few strategies for handling unwelcome questions about his career when he gathers with family. He founded and ran a ski lift ticket platform for 15 years, but it went out of business during the COVID-19 pandemic. Reece then started a career management platform. He’s its sole employee and earns less than he did before.At family parties, he sometimes feels pressure to explain why he doesn’t get a full-time job working for someone else. When he’s asked such questions, he reminds himself that people usually ask because they care.“Oftentimes, if we’re stressed about something that we don’t have an answer to, the question feels like an interrogation, when that’s rarely the intention of the person asking the question,” said Reece, 48, who runs the career management platform Truest.me.A simple “How’s your job going?” can feel like an ambush when you’re unemployed, underemployed or working in jobs your friends and relatives don’t understand or may regard as frivolous. These queries can bring up painful experiences like layoffs. Advice can sound like criticism to recent graduates in a seemingly impenetrable job market, while curiosity about someone’s income can feel like judgment.Even inquiries motivated by a genuine desire to connect can come across as invasive or awkward in a group setting.With holiday gatherings approaching, here are some tips and potential scripts to help you handle tricky career conversations with relatives and feel less defensive. The same strategies can be applied when faced with scrutiny about getting married or having children. Anticipate questions and strategy responses in advance Have a short, confident response or two ready for the job-related queries you think might come up, said Melody Wilding, an executive coach and author of “Managing Up.”For example, if you’re unemployed, you could say, “I’m taking time to find the right fit and not rushing into something upcoming.” Or if you’ve made an unconventional career move, say, “I know it’s not what everyone would choose, but I’m excited about it,” Wilding said.“Then redirect the conversation nicely. You might say, ‘Tell me about you,’ or ‘I’d love to hear about your recent trip,'” she added. Be a boomerang when fielding questions Turning the inquiries around on the questioner can deflect attention and be entertaining.“If someone is willing to ask you a question that requires tremendous vulnerability out of you, then they should be willing to answer one too,” Reece said.When a relative asks if you’re “still job searching” or “Why did you leave a good job?” get curious before you get defensive, Wilding suggested. Instead of immediately responding to their question, try to understand the motivation behind it by countering, “Why do you ask?” or “What makes you say that?” Wilding said.“Maybe they’re just making conversation, which saves you from launching into a full defense of your choices,” she said. Turn it into a game If someone asks about an unstable job or recent layoff, you can say it’s been challenging and then suggest, “Let’s play a game. Everybody tell a story about the worst job they ever had,” Reece said. “Anybody who’s ever worked has a story. And they’re usually amazing.”For recent graduates or those who are trying to figure out what’s next, you could be honest about your uncertainty and reply, “Everybody go around and talk about a time in their career when they weren’t sure what to do next and what you did,” Reece suggested. Let others take the spotlight Hope Bond, 53, spent a decade working as an editor in the magazine industry. She left the field for a few years to raise her young children, then did some freelance editing jobs. When she sought to return to full-time work in 2020, she couldn’t find a position. Bond began working as a site manager for a movie production location in 2024.She loves the job, despite its erratic hours, instability and hourly pay. But at gatherings with her family of lawyers and bankers, she often felt singled out by probing questions about her work.After years of answering their questions, she now redirects them and encourages others to be the star of the conversation, especially her children.“I stay on the periphery. The younger generations are the ones who are bringing the great energy, so I like them to have the floor,” Bond said. “I don’t insert myself into conversation if we’re talking about career or money. Those are my two boundaries. Even with a family that is loving and supportive and wants the best for me, it is just awkward.” Share context about the job market When people feel scrutinized after layoffs or extended unemployment, Avigail Lev, a psychologist at the Bay Area CBT Center in San Francisco, suggests explaining to family members how the job market has changed and how artificial intelligence has impacted their fields.“The first thing you need to say is to speak to the context that things are different, and the decisions about work are very different right now,” Lev said.Many of Lev’s clients work in technology or at AI companies and worry about losing their jobs, while some have already been laid off, she said.“Some people are very depressed right now about not having work or not knowing what’s next. And having a relative blame you for something that’s not in your control is the last thing that you need right now,” Lev said. Choose what you reveal One way to avoid unnecessary judgment is to choose whom you share details about your professional life with.Rishabh Dutta, 25, of Mumbai, India, quit his marketing job for Bollywood movies after stress and long hours led to hair loss. For the next few months, “everyone was constantly asking me what I was doing, if I had found something else,” he said.The next time Dutta left a job, he kept it to himself for a few months. “I just decided not to tell them, and honestly I don’t regret it,” he said. Share your stories and questions about workplace wellness at cbussewitz@ap.org. Follow AP’s Be Well coverage, focusing on wellness, fitness, diet and mental health at https://apnews.com/hub/be-well. —Cathy Bussewitz, AP Business Writer.
